title: New coating technology could reduce glass usage in photovoltaic modules by up to 40% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
German startup Exxosqel has developed a coating technology that strengthens solar glass by targeting microscopic surface cracks. Developed in collaboration with the Fraunhofer Institute for Silicate Research, the technology could reduce glass weight by up to 40% and overall PV module weight by approximately 30%.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
28 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
German startup Exxosqel, a subsidiary of
, has developed a coating technology designed to improve the mechanical strength of solar glass, enabling the use of thinner glass sheets in photovoltaic modules.
Developed in collaboration with the Fraunhofer Institute for Silicate Research (Fraunhofer ISC), the technology could reduce glass weight by up to 40% while maintaining mechanical performance, according to preliminary test results.
Glass currently accounts for 70% to 80% of a PV module’s total weight. Modules typically weigh between 11 kg/m² and 13 kg/m², although heavier designs can reach approximately 16 kg/m².
Reducing glass thickness could therefore lower raw material consumption, manufacturing energy requirements and associated emissions, while also reducing transport and installation loads.
Targeting microscopic glass defects
According to Exxergy, the technology addresses one of the main factors limiting the mechanical strength of flat glass: microscopic cracks that develop during manufacturing and handling. Rather than simply covering surface defects, the coating is designed to penetrate the cracks and modify their mechanical behavior.
The process uses a multicomponent composite material that forms a three-dimensional cross-linked structure. Once applied, the coating matrix establishes covalent bonds at the molecular level within the microcracks. The aim is to inhibit crack propagation and increase the energy required to fracture the glass.
Laboratory tests have shown substantial improvements in mechanical strength. Following several adjustments to the material formulation and application process, 2 mm-thick glass samples exhibited four times the strength of an untempered reference sample. For 1 mm-thick samples, strength increased sevenfold.
The results suggest that the technology could enable thinner glass in PV modules, where conventional strengthening methods face technical limitations.
Limitations of conventional tempering
Thermal tempering is a widely used method for strengthening flat glass. It involves controlled cooling to generate compressive stress at the surface, helping to prevent crack propagation.
However, the process becomes less effective as glass thickness decreases. A nominal thickness of 3.2 mm remains common in PV modules, while achieving sufficient strength with glass measuring 2 mm or less is more challenging using conventional thermal tempering.
Chemical strengthening through ion exchange offers another option. The process replaces sodium ions at the glass surface with potassium ions, generating compressive stress in the surface layer.
Although chemical strengthening can be applied to thin glass and produces fewer optical distortions than thermal tempering, it is more complex and requires more time and energy. Applying the process to large glass sheets also presents challenges.
Exxergy’s technology takes a different approach by targeting the microscopic defects responsible for crack propagation.
Up to 30% reduction in module weight
According to company estimates, reducing glass weight by up to 40% could lower the total weight of a PV module by approximately 30%, depending on its configuration.
For a relatively heavy module weighing 16 kg/m², this would translate into a reduction to approximately 11 kg/m².
Lighter modules could also reduce structural requirements, allowing mounting systems to be designed for lower static loads. The resulting weight savings could further reduce material consumption and ease transport, handling and installation.
The main challenge now is scaling up the technology for industrial applications. Development has so far focused primarily on small glass samples, with the next phase involving larger glass formats and, eventually, full-size commercial PV modules.
Exxergy and Fraunhofer ISC are working to scale up material synthesis, coating application and automation to enable integration into existing production lines. Fraunhofer ISC is contributing its expertise in material synthesis at volumes of up to 100 liters, as well as coating technologies.
According to Exxergy, the technology has reached technology readiness level (TRL) 6. The company said it has produced prototypes in standardized dimensions under near-operational conditions, with mechanical load testing ongoing. The next goal is to reach TRL 7 by validating the coating in an operational environment.
The development work has been supported by the “Green Solar Modules” and “Green Solar Modules Glass II” projects, funded by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and Exxergy.

title: Ricoh announces GW-scale perovskite solar cell production in Japan - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Japan’s Ricoh plans to begin producing perovskite solar cells by 2030, initially targeting annual capacity of several hundred megawatts. The company will use its proprietary inkjet printing technology to streamline manufacturing and reduce production costs.
Emiliano Bellini
28 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Perovskite solar cells manufactured with Ricoh’s inkjet technology
Japanese imaging and electronics company
has announced plans to begin producing perovskite solar cells in Japan by 2030.
The factory will be located at Ricoh Industry Co., Ltd.’s Tohoku site in Shibata, Miyagi prefecture, northern Japan, and will use a manufacturing process based on Ricoh’s proprietary inkjet technology. “With future expansion to GW-scale production in mind, Ricoh aims to establish annual production capacity of several hundred MW by 2030,” the company said in a statement.
Ricoh said its inkjet technology enables precise control over microscopic droplets, allowing materials to be deposited in the required quantities at specific locations. By using the technology to pattern-print all functional layers of perovskite solar cells, the company aims to improve material utilization, simplify manufacturing processes, increase productivity and reduce production costs.
“Ricoh has pursued research and development of organic solar cells based on organic photoconductor technologies developed through the innovation of its multifunction printers,” the company said. “Technologies cultivated through these efforts are now being applied to perovskite solar cells.”
Ricoh said the combination of inkjet printing and substrate transport technologies developed for commercial printing enables continuous, high-speed processing of roll-to-roll substrates, increasing production throughput while reducing manufacturing costs.
In November 2025, Ricoh
announced
that its perovskite solar cells would undergo testing aboard the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s (JAXA) unmanned HTV-X1 cargo spacecraft. The two-month demonstration was designed to assess power generation, electrical performance and durability under space conditions. Ricoh has been developing perovskite solar cells for space applications in collaboration with JAXA since 2017.
The company previously tested its perovskite solar technology aboard the Denden-01 satellite, launched in 2024 for a six-month evaluation. Ricoh has identified low-light performance, resistance to cosmic radiation and the potential for lightweight, flexible designs as key advantages of perovskite solar cells for space applications.
In September 2025, Ricoh also
joined a five-year research project
with Daiwa House Industry and NTT Anode Energy to develop perovskite solar technology for building-integrated and building-attached PV applications. The project, backed by Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO), focuses on improving manufacturing processes and developing installation solutions for rooftops of logistics facilities and exterior walls of data centers.
Ricoh’s move follows that of Japanese electronics manufacturer Panasonic, which last week began
commercial sales of its glass-based perovskite solar panels
, ahead of the planned launch of full-scale mass production in April 2029.
The commercialization efforts come as the Japanese government seeks to establish a domestic perovskite solar industry. In November 2024, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
announced a target
of deploying around 20 GW of perovskite solar capacity by 2040.
The government also outlined plans to support domestic manufacturing and reduce production costs to JPY 14 ($0.09)/W by 2030 and JPY 10/W by 2040. In September 2025, the Ministry of the Environment
introduced subsidy programs
to support early deployment of perovskite solar cells and their integration with battery storage systems.
Japan has since stepped up its support for the technology. In May 2026, NEDO
opened a supplementary funding call
under its Green Innovation Fund to advance mass-production technologies for single-junction perovskite solar cells.
In September, the Ministry of the Environment
announced plans
to exclude conventional silicon solar panels from newly introduced subsidy programs starting in fiscal 2027, prioritizing perovskite and other next-generation solar technologies. The policy shift is intended to strengthen Japan’s industrial competitiveness and accelerate the commercialization of emerging photovoltaic technologies.

title: Organic solar device sets world record making hydrogen from sunlight
content: Scientists have found a way to produce clean green hydrogen using little more than sunshine and water. A team in South Korea has built a solar-powered device that splits water molecules completely on its own. By doing so, it has set a world record in efficiency for organic water-splitting devices. Plus, it runs without any external electrical supply.Traditionally, hydrogen production has relied on natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide in the process. In this regard, solar-powered devices offer a truly zero-emission alternative. However, such devices struggled to generate enough voltage on their own and required outside electricity.“Photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting offers a direct route to solar hydrogen, but organic semiconductor-based photocathodes have been limited by insufficient photovoltage and interfacial instability,” said the researchers in the study.Now, a research team at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) has tried to solve this bottleneck. The researchers have designed a tandem device that stacks two light-absorbing layers on top of each other.Engineering a resilient tandem architectureIn lab trials, the tiny cell reached a solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 7.9%. That marks the highest figure ever recorded for an organic semiconductor photocathode operating without an applied electrical bias.Splitting water requires a minimum electrical threshold of 1.23 volts. Single-layer organic materials cannot reliably reach this target. In the past, stacking two layers to boost voltage caused rapid degradation. The standard connector, a material known as PEDOT:PSS, is highly acidic and vulnerable to water, meaning it quickly damages the neighboring components.The UNIST team replaced this corrosive link with an entirely new hybrid layer. They combined molybdenum oxide with an organic molecule called 2PACz. The molybdenum oxide is neither acidic nor prone to absorbing moisture. It also forms a protective shield that stops liquid solvents from leaking through during the coating process. At the same time, the 2PACz molecules smooth out microscopic defects, allowing electrical charges to flow freely.“The resulting tandem photocathodes reach an onset potential of 1.67 V vs. RHE and a 7.9% solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency under unbiased two-electrode operation, which, to our knowledge, is the highest reported for organic semiconductor-based photocathodes operating without external bias,” added the study.After 10 hours of continuous operation, it retained 86% of its initial photocurrent, whereas conventional designs saw their performance crash to 36%.Minimizing use of precious metalsThe technology has already moved beyond the laboratory bench. The researchers assembled an outdoor module spanning 320 square centimeters, which successfully churned out hydrogen under natural sunlight.To keep costs down, the engineers drastically scaled back their use of precious metals. Platinum was reduced to just 0.1% by weight on the hydrogen electrode, while the counter electrode relied on an affordable nickel-iron-cobalt catalyst. Because both sides work within the same chemical bath, the setup avoids expensive ion-exchange membranes altogether. Economic modeling suggests that if the device can reach its theoretical 16% efficiency limit at scale, it could deliver hydrogen at $4.26 per kilogram.Meanwhile, researchers at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore are taking solar fuel production in an intriguing new direction. Their leaf-inspired device uses sunlight to extract hydrogen directly from seawater while simultaneously neutralizing hydrazine, a toxic industrial chemical. Together, both breakthroughs signal that solar-driven chemistry is rapidly maturing from a fragile concept into a practical industrial tool.

title: US screens 724 metal mixtures to develop new nuclear reactor alloy
content: A team of US researchers has come up with a novel metal alloy for nuclear fission reactors that can reportedly withstand stresses of up to 600 megapascals (MPa) at room temperature.The experimental alloy, called V555, was developed at the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL). The scientists went through nearly 1,000 potential metal combinations to identify the most promising formula for the new alloy. To rapidly screen, simulate, as well as optimize the materials, the scientists used a computational approach called robust alloy design (RAD). It can identify materials that could withstand the extreme temperatures, radiation, and mechanical stress found inside nuclear reactors.PNNL said that the alloy has undergone initial room-temperature tests. “The work has developed into a pathway for the nuclear materials community to explore and evaluate a broader range of materials for future nuclear systems,” Osman El Atwani, PhD, a materials scientist and study leader, said. New reactor materialsTraditional cladding materials include steels and zirconium-based alloys, such as Zircaloy. However, as per El Atwani, new alloys from multiple principal elements could have better properties through changes in their metal composition. To select different elements and create entirely new compositions, he and his team created the eight-step RAD process. It evaluates potential materials against several requirements, such as radiation resistance and manufacturability.Pacific Northwest National Laboratory materials scientists Mohan Nartu using an arc melter to make a new alloy sample called V555.Credit: Eddie Pablo / Pacific Northwest National LaboratoryThe group initially identified around 724 alloy compositions with promising traits by relying on the approach. They then turned to the RAD scoring system to narrow the selection. The assessment tool ranks alloys based on their suitability for nuclear reactors. The team eventually selected V555 for initial lab tests to see if the computational approach could work in practice.“The standard practice is swapping this element with that, and that element with this,” Mohan Nartu, PhD, a PNNL materials scientist who worked on the project, revealed. “While that technically gives you a new material, you didn’t change the broth, so the soup is still old. You’re still going to be somewhat limited.”A strong metal alloyAfter selecting V555, the team made samples to test its structure and strength. To their surprise, initial room-temperature tests showed an estimated yield strength, which refers to the amount of stress a material can withstand before it begins to permanently deform, of approximately 500 to 600 MPa.While the early results showed the alloy’s strength, more tests are needed to confirm whether it can be used in nuclear reactors. The team also found that unused V555 material could be recycled to produce additional samples without affecting their quality. This could reduce the material waste during experimental testing.Pacific Northwest National Laboratory materials scientist Osman El Atwani holds a flat sample of a new alloy called V555 (left) that will be cut into a smaller sample (right) for strength testing.Credit: Eddie Pablo / Pacific Northwest National LaboratoryThe researchers will now examine how V555 withstands heat, radiation, and other reactor conditions. They will also test additional compositions identified through the RAD process. The research was backed by the DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy through its Innovative Nuclear Materials program.“We wanted to show that you can actually choose elements from scratch, if you have the right criteria in mind, and can systematically design a material for nuclear applications,” Nartu concluded in a press release. The study has been published in the journal Materials & Design.

title: 5-MW swappable nuclear reactor prepares for offshore ship integration
content: Nuclear-powered offshore vessels have moved a step closer to reality. A Norwegian project has secured fresh state funding to build and test atomic engines for commercial ships.The Research Council of Norway has awarded $2 million to the Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project. The consortium plans to develop and deploy small, modular nuclear reactors designed specifically to replace fossil fuels in offshore shipping. The reactors are intended to deliver high power output and long operating range without frequent refueling stops.Engineers will not start by placing active nuclear materials straight onto the water. Instead, the team is building an integrated land-based testing facility at Stette, near Ålesund, with trials scheduled to begin in 2027.The Stette facility will run a full-scale replica of a ship’s power plant. To assess safety and performance without radiation risks, engineers will heat the system with electricity rather than atomic fuel. “Testing will cover normal operation, rapid changes in power demand, transient and stress conditions, system performance and crew interaction,” explained the company.Using the Gem microreactorThe system will use the Gem Microreactor. It is a 5-megawatt unit developed by Emerald Nuclear. The design uses TRISO fuel pellets, which coat enriched uranium in layers of ceramic and carbon. “The MarNuPS Pilot will integrate Emerald Nuclear’s 5 MWe Gem Microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems,” noted the firm. This structure withstands extreme heat without melting, preventing the radioactive releases associated with older reactor technologies. The reactor will convert heat into electricity through specialized power conversion systems supplied by Peregrine Turbine Technologies.Under the current plan, the reactor operates inside a sealed unit that is swapped out every five to 15 years, avoiding the need for complex refueling procedures inside ports.Commercial sea deploymentNorwegian shipowner Island Offshore intends to be the first operator to take the system to sea. The company plans to install an operational Gem reactor aboard an offshore service vessel between 2031 and 2032, paving the way for commercial atomic shipping across the North Sea.“Nuclear energy has the potential to provide a new route to decarbonizing offshore vessels without compromising the power, endurance and operational flexibility these ships require,” said Tommy Walaunet, CEO of Island Offshore.“Our role is to ensure that the system is developed around real offshore operations and the people who will ultimately use it.”Leading the industrial consortiumEmerald Nuclear Norway leads the industrial consortium alongside several prominent European maritime and engineering organizations. Shipbuilder VARD Group will manage vessel design and naval architecture, while Vard Electro handles power distribution and control networks.Academic partners are running the underlying simulations. The Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) is modeling reactor physics and thermal hydraulics, while Imperial College London examines structural integrity under dynamic sea conditions. Engineering firm Maskindynamikk will oversee condition monitoring and system diagnostics.Partners have committed substantial private capital alongside the state award. The initial development phase carries an estimated budget of $15.6 million.

title: EV battery-grade lithium extracted by membranes that mimic living cells
content: A new membrane mimics biological cell transport to extract lithium faster, cleaner, and more efficiently.The University of Texas at Austin designed bioinspired nanoscale artificial channels embedded in membranes. The tiny synthetic pores let lithium ions pass through while blocking competing ions (sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium). “Lithium is in our phones, our cars, and the power grid, but getting it out of the ground cleanly is still a hard problem. Our goal is a process that is faster, cleaner, and easier to run,” said Manish Kumar, a professor in the Fariborz Maseeh Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering and the McKetta Department of Chemical Engineering.Synthetic cell-like channelsExisting purification methods depend on evaporation ponds, long processing timelines, and harsh chemicals that generate toxic environmental waste. Finding efficient, eco-friendly ways to separate lithium from these competing ions is important in times of growing supply chain issues.Off late, various solutions have already been emerging from around the world. In this new work, the Texas team turned to biology for a faster solution.It focused on artificial nanoscale channels that mimic the selective biological doors found in living cells. According to the study, the synthetic pores were made from ring-shaped pillar[5]arene molecules with specialized chemical “handles” at their entrances. This act as a precise bouncer, filtering out lithium ions from competing elements. Under an electric field, these channels achieve extraordinary precision. Conservative estimates place the channels’ selectivity at 94 times more likely to transport lithium over sodium, and over 280 times more selective against bulky magnesium ions. Overall, these tiny pores proved two to five times more selective for lithium than other recently reported artificial transporters.“We report the design of a class of bioinspired supramolecular membrane channels that achieve one of the highest overall Li+ selectivities reported to date for artificial transmembrane ion channels, with conservative lower-limit selectivity estimates of Li+/Na+ ≥ 94, Li+/K+ ≥ 136, Li+/Mg2+ ≥ 286,” the study paper noted.Further testing is neededFurther, molecular simulations reveal how the channels perform this atomic screening. As ions enter the narrow pathway, lithium easily trades its surrounding water shell for a favorable handoff with the channel’s chemical entrance. But heavyweight imposters like calcium and magnesium hold onto their water molecules too tightly. Stripping those water shells off requires too much energy, leaving them stranded outside while lithium glides through.The development could set a new performance benchmark for artificial ion channels, paving the way for faster, cleaner, and localized lithium extraction.“We now have a toolkit rather than a one-off result,” said Harekrushna Behera, a research scientist in Kumar’s lab. “By understanding how ions interact with the chemical groups at the channel entrance, we can work toward designing more selective channels for lithium and potentially other critical minerals.”Up next, researchers plan to pack millions of these channels into flexible polymer or lipid membranes to enable continuous, solvent-free separation. If they scale up and succeed in real-world brine tests, the bioinspired membranes could redefine direct lithium extraction (DLE). The technology holds promise for harvesting lithium from discarded EV batteries or even lining the inside of next-generation batteries to boost performance and safety.

title: Autonomous aircraft team up for major search-and-rescue milestone
content: A plane searched for a missing person while a helicopter prepared to carry out an evacuation. Above and alongside them, virtual drones joined a coordinated rescue exercise, with one human directing the entire autonomous team.The demonstration took place near Ottawa in May 2026 and brought together a Ribbit-operated Cessna 150, a Bell 412EP helicopter operated by the National Research Council of Canada (NRC), and multiple simulated drones. Ribbit announced the results on October 27, highlighting how different aircraft could divide tasks and work toward a shared objective.Safety pilots remained aboard both physical aircraft, but the flights were executed autonomously. The exercise tested coordination at both the mission level, where tasks and objectives are managed, and the platform level, where individual aircraft carry out their flights.Search and evacuation duties dividedDuring the mock mission, the Cessna flew search patterns to locate a missing person. It updated and modified its flight plan using a common operating picture, so its movements reflected information shared across the team.After the person was located, the helicopter performed a casualty evacuation. The airplane remained overhead, continuing to provide situational awareness while the helicopter carried out its part of the exercise.Virtual drones added further complexity to the search effort. These simulated aircraft flew alongside the real helicopter and airplane, expanding the number of assets involved without requiring additional physical drones.The division of responsibilities demonstrated how fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft could contribute different capabilities to the same operation while remaining under shared human direction.Ribbit claims specific autonomy firstAccording to Ribbit, the demonstration marked the first time a helicopter, airplane, and virtual aircraft accomplished a shared goal through mission and platform autonomy commanded by a single human.That claim concerns the particular combination of aircraft and autonomy demonstrated, rather than autonomous search and rescue broadly.“By combining research with technology, we successfully demonstrated autonomous aircraft working together toward a shared mission. This collaboration highlights the power of Canadian innovation in advancing next-generation aviation capabilities,” said Derek Gowanlock, program director for Aurora Shield at the NRC.The trial combined Ribbit’s fixed-wing autonomy work with the NRC’s rotary-wing capabilities through the council’s new Drone Innovation Hub.Partnership targets broader operational missionsThe demonstration follows more than three years of collaboration between Ribbit and the NRC. During that period, Ribbit has been contracted to test autonomous technology for priority missions spanning joint operations, tactical aviation, and public safety.Those applications make aircraft coordination, alongside autonomous flight itself, an important area of development.In this exercise, the search aircraft continued supporting the mission after locating the person, rather than ending its role when the helicopter took over.“Today’s milestone was accomplished with impeccable speed and coordination between government and industry. I am extremely proud of what our teams have achieved, and look forward to continuing our work with NRC and DND/CAF,” said Ribbit CEO Carl Pigeon.His statement pointed to further collaboration, although the announcement provided no timetable for subsequent trials or operational deployment.

title: US tests XQ-67A drone with sensors and beyond-line-of-sight data links
content: The US Air Force’s XQ-67A uncrewed aircraft has demonstrated integrated mission systems and beyond-line-of-sight data links during a test flight. The demonstration aimed to improve how uncrewed aircraft support crewed fighters by extending their reach, enhancing situational awareness, and reducing risks to pilots. The project brings together the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and Air Combat Command (ACC) to accelerate the development and delivery of uncrewed combat capabilities.“By pairing AFRL’s rapid prototyping with ACC’s operational test units, the Air Force is shortening the timeline between concept and warfighter capability,” said Col. Matthew Caspers, Deputy Technology Executive Officer for Air at the Department of the Air Force (DAF), in a statement.XQ-67A tests autonomyThe US Air Force has flown its XQ-67A Autonomous Collaborative Platform (ACP) at the Nevada Test and Training Range, demonstrating the integration of advanced mission systems and beyond-line-of-sight communication technology. The test focused on technologies designed to help uncrewed aircraft operate across distributed theaters and support crewed fighter formations in demanding combat environments.During the flight, the XQ-67A demonstrated the integration of several mission-critical systems, including advanced sensors, mission computers, and power and thermal management hardware. These components are designed to work together in demanding operational environments, providing the aircraft with the onboard technology needed to support autonomous missions.Sensors collect information about the aircraft’s surroundings, while mission computers process data and support mission-related functions. Integrating these systems into a common platform is important for developing uncrewed aircraft that can gather, process, and communicate information during operations.The flight also tested power and thermal management hardware, which helps manage the electrical and heat loads generated by onboard equipment. These functions are particularly important when multiple advanced systems operate together, as they must remain within their operating limits to support reliable performance.Rather than evaluating individual components in isolation, the demonstration focused on integrating these technologies within the XQ-67A. The test provided an opportunity to assess how the systems work together as part of an autonomous aircraft architecture.Tests data linksAnother key element of the demonstration was the integration of beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) data links. These communication systems enable information to be transmitted beyond the direct line of sight between communicating platforms, supporting operations over greater distances.The test combined the data links with live, virtual, and constructive (LVC) simulations. This approach brings together real-world activities, simulated environments, and computer-generated elements to evaluate how systems and operational units can function together.According to the AFRL, the demonstration showed how uncrewed platforms could be managed across distributed theaters using resilient, layered command and control. Such capabilities are intended to help military forces coordinate operations across geographically separated areas while maintaining access to combat-relevant information.The flight also evaluated autonomous architectures aligned with the Autonomy and Agile Mission Suite Government Reference Architectures. These government reference architectures provide a common technical framework for developing and integrating autonomous systems and mission software.The Air Force said the XQ-67A’s systems were able to process and relay combat-relevant data in real-world scenarios. This capability is central to efforts to develop uncrewed aircraft that can exchange information and operate as part of a broader force rather than functioning as isolated platforms.The XQ-67A is being developed as part of the Air Force’s broader effort to advance Autonomous Collaborative Platforms. These uncrewed aircraft are intended to complement crewed combat aircraft by extending their operational reach, improving situational awareness, and increasing the number of available aircraft.By deploying uncrewed platforms alongside crewed fighters, military commanders could gain additional operational capacity without requiring a pilot in every aircraft. The approach is also intended to reduce the exposure of human aircrews to dangerous missions. The demonstration supports the US Department of the Air Force’s efforts to develop systems that can deliver greater operational reach and more resilient command and control in complex combat environments.

title: Scientists recover 90% of scarce metal from flame-retardant e-waste
content: Researchers from Rice University have developed a new fast-heating method to recover approximately 90 percent of Antimony from plastic electronic waste.​​Antimony is the element behind the flame-retardant capacity of plastic casing that is used in electronic devices to prevent the risk of electrical fires.In this new method, the team electronically heated the plastic waste generated from their lab briefly at high temperatures, which allowed antimony to evaporate and condense in the collection area.​Plus, the plastic spent only 9.4 milliseconds between 392 and 932 degrees Fahrenheit, leaving little time for organic bromides to form toxic compounds.Antimony is rapidly depleting, as nearly 39 percent of global supplies are consumed in manufacturing flame-retardant plastics, most of which ultimately end up in landfills. Global flame-retardant production is projected to reach 82 million metric tons in 2030, alongside tens of millions of tons of annual electronic waste. This escalating demand poses a severe threat to future mineral reserves.Flash heating holds key​Cutting off at the pass, U.S. researchers explored ways to recapture this important raw material that ends up in the heaps of e-waste after the end of life of the electronic devices.​Traditional recovery methods use slow heating to release the metal before capture. This poses a huge environmental and health risk because such treatments release toxic organic bromides, which are another key component of flame-retardant plastics in forms that are difficult to capture.​”Conventionally, heating the plastic releases the antimony in a volatile and difficult-to-collect form as well as creating and releasing hazardous organic bromide compounds,” said Leo Haoxin Ye, the first author of this paper and a graduate student in James Tour’s lab at Rice. “Other options are risky or more impractical, such as using strong acids, organic solvents, or multistep treatment options.”​According to the team, slowly heating a material allows the element to change form and create new compounds, which could be hazardous.​Recognizing slow heating as the culprit, the team turned to Tour’s flash heating method. It heats the material in just a few milliseconds, rapidly raising its temperature to hundreds of degrees Celsius. The improved method was called isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating. It was adapted for efficient antimony recovery while also capturing the hazardous organic bromide.“We found flame-retardant plastic waste generated by our own laboratory, ground it up and then placed it between two sheets of electrically heated carbon paper. We used ultrafast heating to pulse-heat it several times,” Ye said.Reduced toxic byproducts​Exposing plastic to high temperatures for only 9.4 milliseconds prevents the formation of toxic organic bromides. Researchers converted 83 percent of the bromide into hydrogen bromide, a valuable industrial chemical. Further, testing the method on power-supply housings, printed circuit boards, and electrical connectors proved successful across multiple types of flame-retardant plastics. The process conserves critical antimony supplies while simultaneously regenerating bromide salts for reuse.The team concluded by stating that the “isothermal-clamped flash Joule heating could improve the speed, safety, and practicality of antimony recovery from discarded flame-retardant plastics.” ​The findings were published in a Nature Chemical Engineering study.​

title: US Navy's CHAOS cruise missile gets rocket boosters from X-Bow
content: US defense manufacturer X-Bow Systems has been selected to develop and produce rocket boosters for the US Navy’s new ground-launched cruise missile program. It aims to give American allies a more affordable way to strike land and maritime targets.On October 27, X-Bow Systems announced that prime contractor CoAspire chose it to supply solid rocket boosters for the Navy’s CHAOS missile program.Reportedly, CoAspire bases the CHAOS missile on its larger RAACM-ER design, claiming an undemonstrated potential range of up to 1,000 nautical miles, or roughly 1,150 miles.The value of X-Bow’s subcontract, the number of boosters involved, and the delivery schedule have not been disclosed. The selection is part of a broader Navy effort to develop scalable, exportable precision-strike weapons for allied countries, potentially reducing their dependence on expensive legacy missile inventories.How the CHAOS cruise missile will launch from the groundThe CHAOS program’s initial configuration is designed for ground launch, letting forces deploy the cruise missile from a launcher rather than relying on a fighter jet or warship to launch it.X-Bow will build the solid rocket motors that accelerate the weapon out of its launcher and provide the initial thrust needed to get it moving. Once the booster has done its job, the cruise missile’s own propulsion system can sustain its flight toward the target.The weapon is based on CoAspire’s Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile-Extended Range (RAACM-ER). In a July announcement, CoAspire said the Navy selected the ground-launched variant under a $70 million prototype agreement. The missile system is intended to engage both land-based targets and moving maritime targets.The Navy’s August announcement says the initial expeditionary ground-launch capability is expected to enter production by 2028. The program could subsequently expand to surface-launch platforms, with air-launched configurations also possible depending on military requirements.Navy wants affordable weapons for its alliesThe Navy’s Precision Strike Weapons program office is developing CHAOS under PMX-201, with affordability, production scale, and exportability built into its requirements.The program is intended to give allied forces access to modern precision-strike capabilities without requiring them to rely exclusively on costly existing weapons. The Navy is also using agreements designed to speed prototype development and encourage competition from newer defense companies.CoAspire is one of two companies selected for the initial CHAOS effort, alongside Zone 5 Technologies. The Navy says its approach is designed to accommodate partner countries’ requirements from the outset and potentially allow local assembly and industrial participation. No allied customers or final procurement quantities have been announced for the system.X-Bow expands its rocket motor businessThe CHAOS selection adds to a busy year for X-Bow, which says it has secured seven new propulsion programs in 2026 across the Navy, Army, and Missile Defense Agency.The company uses additive manufacturing techniques to produce solid rocket motors, arguing that its approach can help increase output and reduce manufacturing costs. It recently completed a major production contract involving more than 2,100 rocket motors, according to its announcement.X-Bow has also been selected to supply booster motors for the Army’s Low-Cost Containerized Munition program through contractor Leidos. This is another effort focused on producing affordable cruise-missile capabilities at scale.

title: Scientists speed up tests to protect satellite chips from radiation
content: Human experts working alongside agentic AI are building the foundation for lighter, longer-lasting satellites. Scientists at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) are accelerating the development of “radiation-hardened” (rad-hard) materials using Super Intelligence (SI) and automation.These materials are built to withstand high-radiation environments, such as space and nuclear reactors. Radiation-induced failures in these components can delay or cancel missions, making radiation hardening important for decade-long operations.“Space is a highly energetic environment, with heavy ions and other particles bombarding our devices. Agentic workflows come at a time when there is a need for better rad-hard testing techniques,” said scientist Erin Barker. SciLink AI systemResearchers are studying layered aluminum gallium nitride and gallium nitride chips that power satellites, communications, radar, and power systems. Before a microchip ever tastes the void of space, it is manufactured in a clean facility where even a single stray speck of dust could mean instant failure. Once launched into space on a satellite, that delicate microchip enters a dangerous environment filled with constant, invisible radiation. Galactic cosmic rays, heavy ions, and near-light-speed electrons pepper the cosmos.One bad exposure can scramble a satellite’s memory, send a spacecraft off course, or completely kill an expensive weather or communications mission.Testing how materials handle space environments has long been a slow and tedious process. To prevent these orbital catastrophes, PNNL researchers are changing how we shield space electronics. This new work accelerated the development of radiation-hardened microchips using a multi-agent AI system named SciLink. This intelligent software hierarchy evaluates microscopic radiation damage in just a few hours. It could replace analytical work that previously took human teams weeks.Physical shielding or backup systems protect electronics, but extra weight raises launch costs and reduces overall mission efficiency. Therefore, making the microchips themselves radiation-resistant may be a more practical solution.Protecting satellite microchipsAchieving this requires testing advanced chips made from aluminum gallium nitride and gallium nitride under extreme simulated conditions.Using ion-beam experiments at the University of Tennessee to mimic years of cosmic radiation in hours, PNNL researchers generated massive, complex datasets. Normally, integrating data from instruments like atom probe tomography and scanning transmission electron microscopy takes weeks.SciLink organizes its AI agents into a corporate hierarchy led by three “project leads” overseeing experimental analysis, planning, and computational simulation. In interactive sessions, these AI leads debate hypotheses, synthesize multi-instrument data, evaluate damage mechanisms, and propose follow-up experiments. “The system allows us to take into account all the measurements to piece together what has happened, to understand the damage that has occurred and why it happened,” said Jenna Pope, a PNNL scientist. “It’s like having several people who did different forms of testing come together and discuss the results — only it’s an agent pulling together the information instantly.”The AI also assigns numerical confidence scores to every conclusion. In recent tests, SciLink reported a 90 percent confidence score that heavy ions dominated the primary microchip damage. It also signaled a cautious 60 percent confidence regarding proton-induced defects, letting researchers know exactly where to dig deeper.Despite the blinding speed of agentic workflows, experts stress that humans remain firmly in the loop to design experiments, run calculations, and double-check AI findings for hallucinations. And even scientist Barker asserts, “Intelligent agents are a tremendous help, but you can’t just turn your brain off.”

title: US-developed SPINE uses machine learning to decode neutrino science
content: US researchers at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have developed the Scalable Particle Imaging with Neural Embeddings (SPINE). It is a machine learning tool to analyze data from experiments designed to find neutrinos, the elusive ghost particle. The tool recently analyzed its first set of data from a real-world experiment and is prepared to tackle data from more ambitious projects in the future. Neutrinos are extremely abundant particles in our universe but are the most elusive. These nearly massless particles are released by stars and and radioactive elements alike but rarely interact with matter. Despite their abundance, these have been very difficult to detect. So, scientists have built large particle accelerators and complex detectors to catch these ghostly particles. A typical neutrino detector holds hundreds of tons of liquid argon cooled to temperatures of -300 degrees Fahrenheit (-184 degrees Celsius). When a neutrino strikes an argon atom, it sends several particles traveling through the liquid and leaves a trail of electrons that are picked up by collection wires to create a three-dimensional image of the event. Reconstructing the event with SPINECapturing the image is only the beginning, since scientists must reconstruct the event from a complex picture generated by data from the collection wires, overlapping signals, and background activity, which can include multiple neutrino interactions at the same time. Conventionally, scientists have done this using special algorithms that chain events together one step at a time. Each algorithm performs a narrow task and passes it to the next. However, this carries a significant risk: an error at any step can carry forward through the rest of the computation. To address this, researcher François Drielsma, a scientist at SLAC, used a different approach in which multiple machine-learning models work together to reconstruct the event. Different models perform different tasks such as spotting basic features in the image, identifying individual particles, and then piecing together the complete interaction. The work began as a postdoctoral position at SLAC in 2015-16 and has been expanded into a program that will eventually be deployed on eight different detectors in the future. The first testMuch of SPINE’s work so far consisted of simulations to test whether the approach works. More recently, the team got their hands on real-world data from ICARUS, the largest detector in the Short-Baseline Neutrino program at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Illinois. Neutrinos are known to oscillate between the three flavors as they travel, but physicists wonder whether if sterile neutrino produces some oscillations that the three flavors cannot explain. Even though the first analysis did not make a major scientific breakthrough, the researchers found that SPINE recovered 60 percent more neutrino interactions that were usable when compared to conventional approaches.With more experiments underway in the Short-Baseline program, SPINE will have more data to analyze later this year and in 2027, but the team has already set its sights on results from the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), which will begin operations by 2030. Under construction, DUNE will send a neutrino beam from Fermilab in Illinois to detectors 800 miles away in South Dakota. The experiment’s near detector is expected to see over 1,000 interactions per 10 seconds as it searches for answers to the matter-antimatter asymmetry.  SPINE is already trained to handle data from DUNE detectors.

title: US set to boost nuclear capacity by 1.1 GW to power 930,000 homes
content: The United States is preparing to provide up to $5 billion in federal loan financing to expand its existing nuclear power fleet. The move comes as surging demand from artificial intelligence drives a search for clean, round-the-clock electricity.The U.S. Department of Energy has announced a provisional funding agreement with Constellation. Under the plan, the energy firm will receive federal backing to overhaul and upgrade eight nuclear facilities. The selected plants, which comprise eight stations across Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania, house multiple reactor units.The upgrades will add nearly 1.1 gigawatts of generation capacity to the power system. That is roughly the output of a brand-new commercial reactor, achieved entirely by boosting the efficiency and hardware of current plants.“These investments will add more reliable baseload power to the grid, help lower electricity costs, strengthen our nation’s energy security, and fuel long-term American prosperity,” said EDF Director Gregory A. Beard.Tech-driven power demandThe expansion comes as the tech sector races to secure dependable power for massive data centers. Running advanced artificial intelligence models requires continuous, baseload electricity. While wind and solar farms are expanding rapidly, their output fluctuates with the weather. Nuclear reactors, by contrast, run day and night without emitting carbon during generation.Energy planners expect the additional 1.1 gigawatts to deliver enough power for more than 930,000 households. The initiative is also forecast to create more than 10,000 engineering and construction jobs. The electricity will feed directly into two major regional networks. These are the PJM Interconnection in the east and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator across the central United States.Six plants across Illinois will see equipment upgrades: Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle, and Quad Cities. Work is also scheduled for the Limerick station in Pennsylvania and the Calvert Cliffs plant in Maryland.Rigorous technical evaluationsThe federal loan offer is not yet finalized. Before any funds are released, Constellation must clear rigorous technical evaluations and complete formal environmental reviews. It must also finalize legal agreements with the Department of Energy’s financing office.Even so, the pledge highlights growing momentum behind existing nuclear infrastructure. Earlier this month, Constellation struck a commercial partnership with Amazon to modernize Calvert Cliffs, Maryland’s sole nuclear power station.That commercial agreement aims to unlock more than $3bn in private infrastructure spending. It will upgrade the 1,790-megawatt plant and add roughly 190 megawatts of fresh zero-carbon capacity between 2030 and 2032.Crucially, the electricity from Calvert Cliffs will remain part of the public grid rather than being walled off exclusively for server farms. Amazon will draw power from the regional grid while helping underwrite the cost of capital improvements.Federal officials noted that the loan package includes options to fund further reactor upgrades at other Constellation sites in the future. For now, the push shows how governments and tech giants are aligning around existing nuclear plants. The goal is to power computing infrastructure without derailing emissions targets.

title: 110 Chinese humanoid robots dance in sync to set Guinness World Record
content: China has set a Guinness World Records title after 110 humanoid robots performed synchronized dance routines. The robots, developed by Chinese robotics company AGIBOT, demonstrated coordinated movements in a large-scale public performance. The event highlights China’s efforts to advance humanoid robotics and expand the commercial deployment of robots across different industries. In August, AGIBOT won 46 medals, including 18 gold, at the second World Humanoid Robot Games, competing in athletics, manipulation, hotel services, and emergency response.Robots create recordA group of 110 humanoid robots developed by AGIBOT has set a Guinness World Records title after performing synchronized dance routines in Jinan, Shandong Province.According to reports, the performance took place on October 24 at the Yellow River International Convention and Exhibition Center. The robots, identified as full-size Expedition A3 models, danced in formation, jumped, and carried out coordinated movements while repeatedly changing positions.During the demonstration, the robots created wave-like patterns and arranged themselves into different formations, including the number 2026. Their movements were coordinated to maintain synchronization as the group transitioned between dance sequences.A hundred AGIbot A3 pic.twitter.com/JF0319qXa7— Eren Chen (@ErenChenAI) October 25, 2026A Guinness World Records adjudicator attended the event to verify the number of participating robots and present an official certificate recognizing the achievement. The record was for the most humanoid robots dancing simultaneously.According to AGIBOT, all 110 robots were standard production models rather than machines specially modified for the event. This detail highlights the company’s use of commercially produced humanoid robots in a large-scale coordinated performance.The demonstration showcases the ability to coordinate a large number of humanoid robots during a complex group activity. It also highlights the role of communication systems and centralized control in managing multiple robotic platforms simultaneously. However, synchronized dancing is a controlled demonstration and does not, by itself, establish how reliably the robots can perform complex tasks in industrial or other real-world environments.Synchronizing robot fleetFor the Guinness performance, AGIBOT robots used the firm’s LinkBots platform, which is designed to coordinate multiple robots through swarm scheduling and cluster control. LinkBots combines communication networks, positioning technology, and control software to manage the movements of multiple robots. Its integration with ultra-wideband (UWB) positioning technology enables centimeter-level tracking of the robots’ relative positions, helping them maintain spacing as they move through different formations.This positioning capability is especially important when robots move in coordinated proximity. Accurate location information helps the system organize formation changes and reduce the risk of collisions during complex sequences.The platform also supports coordinated scheduling, allowing robots to execute assigned movements as part of a larger routine. Rather than requiring operators to control every robot individually, the system is designed to manage group activities through centralized coordination and information about each machine’s state.LinkBots uses 5G and Wi-Fi connectivity to support communication between the robots and the control infrastructure. These networks provide channels for transmitting instructions and coordination data across the fleet.The platform’s reported capabilities also include adjusting formations and planning movements around obstacles. However, publicly available technical details do not fully establish how these functions operate or how extensively they have been tested outside controlled demonstrations.According to experts, the performance highlights AgiBot’s efforts to coordinate commercially produced humanoid robots at scale. It also demonstrates the role of swarm-control systems in managing multiple robotic platforms performing synchronized tasks.

title: Anduril, Qualcomm plan rugged US-made laptop with 90% local components
content: A computer made entirely in the United States, down to its display and smallest components, is the ambition behind Anduril’s latest project.The defense technology company announced a partnership with Qualcomm on Tuesday to develop BlueChip, a rugged laptop that will open for preorders in 2027.The first model will target military personnel, government agencies, first responders, and law enforcement, combining an Arizona-made processor with hardware built for demanding environments. About 90 percent of its components will initially come from the U.S. or allied countries, with founder Palmer Luckey aiming to move the entire supply chain onto American soil eventually.An American chip at the coreBlueChip will use a Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series processor manufactured at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s facility in Arizona. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said the chip shares its architecture with processors used in other laptops, including Microsoft’s Surface devices.However, Anduril has not finalized contracts with every component supplier, and detailed specifications remain unavailable.“As of right now, the laptop’s bill of materials is about 90 percent U.S. and allied [ally countries], and we have a technical roadmap to get to 100 percent domestic over time,” Luckey said.That ambition extends beyond processors and final assembly. Luckey is aiming for produce displays, metal parts, magnetic components, and everything else inside the machine domestically.Some pieces are already falling into place. He said he has identified an American supplier for the glass covering the screen. The display itself remains among the components he says are currently manufactured only in China.Built for government demandsBlueChip’s first customers are expected to value durability and supply-chain transparency over portability. Engineering the laptop to withstand rain, dust, and harsh conditions will add weight and limit battery life.Anduril is positioning the computer for agencies that must purchase U.S.-made equipment. Customers would be able to trace and audit its components, providing greater visibility into where their hardware originates.“These computers are the anti-surveillance computer. You fully control it,” Luckey said in a recent interview. “You know everything that is in it, every single component, and you know every software component that is running on it,” he added.Software compatibility is another priority. Anduril is working to ensure the Arm-based machine supports Windows applications, software built for certain government-used Linux distributions, and older programs that agencies continue to operate. That work will be important for buyers whose existing systems depend on aging applications.A premium for domestic productionAnduril has not announced a price, though Luckey estimates BlueChip could cost about 20 percent more than a typical high-end PC.Consumers will be able to order one, and the company may set up a waiting list. Still, Luckey acknowledged that an ordinary buyer without a specific need for its capabilities would likely find better value elsewhere. He nevertheless sees the laptop as the beginning of a broader BlueChip computer lineup, potentially reaching beyond its initial institutional audience.For now, the challenge is turning that manufacturing ambition into a finished product while securing suppliers for components that remain outside the proposed domestic supply chain.

title: New deck-mounted missile launcher could extend US Navy firepower
content: BAE Systems has tested a new missile launcher designed to help U.S. Navy ships replenish their weapons without returning to port. The Adaptable Deck Launcher (ADL) completed its first live-fire demonstration in California on October 27, 2026. The system could give American warships more flexibility when operating far from established naval bases.The launcher uses existing Mk 41 Vertical Launching System (VLS) technology to simplify integration with established naval equipment. Its design also addresses a persistent challenge for deployed fleets: restoring missile capacity after ships expend their weapons. Faster reloading could help vessels sustain their combat readiness during extended operations.New approach to missile deploymentTraditional vertical launch systems provide warships with an integrated way to fire missiles from onboard launch cells. However, replenishing those weapons at sea remains a significant logistical challenge. Ships may need specialized facilities or port visits to restore their ammunition supplies.The ADL offers another option through a deck-mounted configuration. BAE Systems designed the launcher to use the Mk 41 system’s existing logistics and electronics architecture. This approach could reduce the need for entirely separate support infrastructure.According to BAE Systems, the launcher can accommodate Evolved SeaSparrow Missile (ESSM) Mk 25 quad-pack canisters. Each canister holds four missiles, allowing compatible launch systems to carry multiple interceptors within a single launch cell.The ESSM provides shipboard defenses against supersonic anti-ship missiles, aircraft, and other aerial threats. Compatibility with these canisters gives the ADL a defined role in existing naval air-defense operations.Faster reloading for deployed fleetsThe launcher’s main advantage lies in its potential to replenish missile stocks more quickly. Ships operating in contested waters could benefit from restoring their firepower without making a dedicated trip back to port.BAE Systems says the ADL complements the Mk 41 VLS rather than replacing it. The established system remains a central part of naval missile integration, while the new launcher adds another way to sustain ammunition supplies.Jason Casciotti, vice president of Weapons Systems at BAE Systems, described the live-fire test as a milestone for naval readiness. He said the launcher would give crews more flexibility when maintaining combat loads at sea.The practical benefits will depend on how the Navy integrates the system into its logistics and operational procedures. The initial demonstration establishes a technical milestone, but further testing and evaluation will determine its broader utility.Designed for diverse naval platformsBAE Systems envisions the ADL supporting operations across aircraft carriers, amphibious ships, and other surface combatants. Its modular approach could help the Navy adapt missile deployment capabilities to different ship configurations.The design also targets unmanned naval platforms. Compact launcher configurations could suit medium-sized unmanned surface vessels, which may offer additional options for distributed maritime operations.For the U.S. Navy, distributing weapons across more platforms could provide greater flexibility when planning missions and sustaining operations. Unmanned vessels could potentially carry additional missile capacity without requiring the same onboard crew arrangements as conventional warships.Developed under a U.S. Department of War contract for the NATO Seasparrow Project Office, the ADL expands the options available for naval missile deployment. Its longer-term value will depend on demonstrated reliability, compatibility, and the Navy’s assessment of its reloading capabilities.

title: China's 5,000-mile H-6K bomber spotted with suspected jamming pods
content: China’s H-6K strategic bomber has appeared in images carrying two suspected electronic warfare pods, hinting at a possible upgrade to its long-range strike capabilities. The equipment could help the aircraft interfere with enemy radar without relying entirely on dedicated electronic warfare escorts.The photographs surfaced on social media Saturday, but their authenticity remains unverified. They show two pods mounted beneath the bomber’s wings. Their appearance resembles equipment used by China’s J-16D electronic warfare aircraft, although analysts have not confirmed their identity or operational status.New pods could disrupt radarElectronic warfare pods can interfere with radar signals, making it harder for opposing forces to detect, track, or engage aircraft. Depending on their design, these systems can support missions by disrupting radar coverage or complicating an adversary’s air defense operations.Adding such equipment to the H-6K could give Chinese forces more flexibility during long-range strike missions. The bomber could potentially conduct electronic attacks alongside its existing weapons operations, reducing its dependence on specialized escort aircraft in certain scenarios.However, the available images do not establish whether the pods represent a permanent upgrade, a testing configuration, or an operational capability. Their performance and the radar frequencies they might target also remain unknown.China has previously equipped other H-6 variants with electronic countermeasures. The H-6C served as a specialized electronic warfare aircraft during the 1980s. The H-6G later carried similar equipment, demonstrating that China has explored this role for decades.H-6K remains long-range workhorseThe H-6K entered flight testing in 2007 and remains a central part of the People’s Liberation Army Air Force’s long-range strike fleet. China developed the H-6 family from the Soviet-era Tu-16 bomber, adapting the original design for modern weapons and mission requirements.The H-6K can reportedly travel around 8,000 kilometers (4,970 miles) and carry approximately 12 to 15 metric tons of payload. Its ability to launch weapons from a distance allows it to threaten targets without necessarily entering the immediate engagement range of opposing defenses.Its weapons portfolio includes stand-off cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, including nuclear-capable systems. Earlier this month, Chinese state media released footage showing an H-6K launching a YJ-21 hypersonic anti-ship missile. The YJ-21 reportedly reaches speeds of Mach 8 to Mach 10 and has an estimated range of around 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles). Those figures illustrate the bomber’s potential to deliver weapons against distant maritime targets.J-16D offers important cluesThe suspected pods resemble equipment associated with the RKZ930 family, developed for China’s J-16D electronic attack aircraft. Beijing unveiled the J-16D in 2021, positioning it as a dedicated electronic warfare variant of the J-16 fighter.The aircraft serves a role comparable to the U.S. Navy’s EA-18G Growler, which supports military operations by attacking or disrupting hostile electronic systems. RKZ930 variants feature different shapes and mounting arrangements, including wingtip and underwing installations. Analysts believe the variants address different radar frequency bands, although detailed specifications remain limited. Similar equipment may also support the Chinese Navy’s carrier-based J-15D electronic warfare aircraft.If the H-6K eventually adopts these pods for operational missions, China could expand the bomber’s role beyond delivering long-range weapons.

title: Scientists flip single atom's nuclear spin using radio waves
content: Researchers in the Netherlands have demonstrated that radio waves can control the nuclear spin of a single atom even when it is largely disentangled from the spin of its electrons, challenging existing expectations about how atomic nuclei respond to electrical signals.The experiment, conducted at Delft University of Technology, revealed an unexpected way to manipulate the weak magnetism inside an atomic nucleus. The researchers say the finding could eventually support new approaches to storing and retrieving quantum information.Using a modified scanning tunneling microscope, the team directed precisely controlled electrical signals at an individual atom. They found that a signal targeting the nucleus could flip its spin without relying on the strong coupling between nuclear and electron spins previously thought necessary for this type of manipulation.The result surprised the researchers because nuclear spins are generally much less responsive to external electrical signals than electron spins. Their relative isolation makes them attractive for quantum information storage, but also presents challenges when scientists attempt to control them.Separating two magnetic signalsAtoms contain several sources of magnetism, including the spins of their electrons and, in some cases, their nuclei.Electron spins produce much stronger magnetic effects and are comparatively easy to manipulate. Nuclear spins are weaker and better shielded from their surroundings, making them harder to access directly.Previous experiments at Delft primarily focused on controlling electron spins and observing their influence on nuclear spins through an interaction known as hyperfine coupling.This interaction links the magnetic behavior of electrons and nuclei, allowing changes in one spin to influence the other.In the latest experiment, researchers led by Hester Vennema refined a technique called double magnetic resonance to investigate the two spins separately.They applied two signals simultaneously, with one targeting the electron spin and the other targeting the nuclear spin.By independently adjusting the signals, the team could examine how each component responded.The researchers discovered that the nuclear spin could be flipped even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled.“According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen,” said Sander Otte, who leads the research group.“The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunnelling microscope.”The finding suggests that the mechanism responsible for the observed nuclear-spin transitions is not fully explained by the researchers’ existing model.Tuning individual quantum statesThe experiment relied on magnetic resonance, a technique that uses signals at specific frequencies to change the orientation of magnetic spins.Because quantum spins can occupy only certain states, researchers must apply a signal at the appropriate frequency to induce a transition.Vennema compared the process to playing a guitar string, where each string responds to a particular note.The researchers noted that the frequencies associated with nuclear-spin transitions are typically 100 to 1,000 times lower than those associated with electron spins.By refining double magnetic resonance for a single atom, the team demonstrated a way to address these different magnetic components independently.The ability to manipulate nuclear spins is particularly relevant to quantum information research.Because nuclear spins are relatively isolated from environmental disturbances, they are promising candidates for storing quantum states. However, reliable control and readout remain essential requirements for practical applications.The new experiment demonstrates an additional control mechanism, but it does not establish a working quantum memory or explain precisely how the nuclear spin responds to the applied signal.Further research will be needed to identify the underlying physical mechanism and determine whether the technique can be used reliably in quantum devices.The findings were published in Nature Communications.

title: B-52 bomber's Mach 5 air-launched missile moves toward production
content: Lockheed Martin has secured a $694 million U.S. Air Force contract to manufacture its Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW), advancing efforts to field an air-launched hypersonic strike system. Designed to travel beyond Mach 5, the weapon aims to help American forces engage targets quickly from long distances.The award also brings production capacity into focus. Lockheed Martin has started expanding its facility in Troy, Alabama, to support manufacturing and prepare for larger production volumes. The work follows years of development and testing with the Air Force.Alabama facility expands productionLockheed Martin broke ground on an expansion of Building P-20 in Troy that will add 47,000 square feet of manufacturing space. The project will triple the facility’s existing production area dedicated to ARRW.The expansion is expected to create American jobs over the next four years. It will also equip workers to manufacture the weapon using advanced manufacturing methods, robotics, and digital technologies.Lockheed Martin has committed $67 million to the facility expansion and associated equipment before receiving government funding for the project. The investment forms part of a broader plan to spend $8 billion to $9 billion through 2030 to meet rising demand for munitions.Alabama already hosts nearly 4,000 Lockheed Martin employees. The additional manufacturing space could strengthen the state’s role in the company’s defense production network as the Air Force moves toward larger-scale manufacturing.B-52 carries hypersonic weaponThe Air Force designed ARRW for integration with the B-52 Stratofortress bomber. The combination would allow the aircraft to launch a high-speed weapon against targets from considerable distances, keeping the launch platform away from some threats.Traveling faster than Mach 5 means ARRW can exceed five times the speed of sound. Its hypersonic flight profile is intended to shorten the time available for an adversary to detect, assess, and respond to an incoming strike.Speed alone, however, does not determine a weapon’s effectiveness. ARRW must also withstand intense aerodynamic heating and maintain accuracy throughout its flight.Lockheed Martin says the missile uses advanced materials to manage extreme temperatures. Its onboard technology package is designed to preserve accuracy and lethality, while its capabilities aim to help it overcome a range of defensive systems.These engineering demands make manufacturing readiness an important step. Moving from development and testing into production requires repeatable processes that can deliver complex hardware at the required scale.Production targets strategic capabilityTim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, said the award demonstrates the company’s ability to move advanced systems into production quickly. He described ARRW as a high-precision weapon intended to expand the Air Force’s strike options.Lockheed Martin has continued research and development alongside its preparations for manufacturing. The company says those efforts support the Air Force’s requirement for an air-launched hypersonic weapon.The production contract marks a significant manufacturing milestone, but it does not, by itself, establish how quickly the Air Force will receive operational missiles. Delivery schedules, production quantities, and deployment timelines were not specified in the supplied announcement.The Alabama expansion nevertheless establishes the industrial capacity needed to support the program’s next phase. Its progress will help determine how quickly Lockheed Martin can turn the weapon’s development work into manufactured systems for the U.S. military.

title: New model shifts nuclear power output without slowing reactors
content: Researchers in the US have developed a modeling approach that could allow nuclear power plants to adjust electricity output to changing grid demand without repeatedly reducing reactor power.The system combines molten salt reactors with thermal energy storage, allowing excess heat to be stored when electricity demand is low and used to generate additional power when demand increases.Developed by researchers at the University of Central Florida (UCF), the approach could help nuclear plants operate alongside solar and wind farms, whose electricity production changes with weather conditions and the time of day.The researchers combined thermodynamic modeling with an economic analysis to examine how storing and releasing reactor heat could improve operational flexibility and help nuclear plants respond to fluctuating electricity prices.Storing heat between peaksUnlike solar and wind installations, conventional nuclear power plants are generally designed to produce electricity continuously. Adjusting their output to match rapid changes in demand can introduce operational challenges.As renewable energy contributes a larger share of electricity generation, nuclear plants may need to become more flexible without compromising the steady operation of their reactors.“Nuclear power needs to be flexible while nuclear reactors operate at a steady pace because grid demand varies throughout the day, and this is especially pronounced in grids with high solar penetration, which typically peaks around noon and diminishes toward night,” said Augusto Delavald Marques, a doctoral researcher involved in the study.Thermal energy storage offers a way to separate heat production from electricity generation.Instead of sending all the heat produced by a reactor directly to the power generation system, some could be diverted into storage when electricity demand is low.The stored heat could then be released to produce additional electricity during periods of higher demand.This arrangement would allow the reactor to maintain a relatively steady operating level while the electricity generation system adjusts its output.The researchers focused on molten salt reactors, an advanced nuclear reactor design that uses molten salts in its operation. The study examined how these reactors could be integrated with thermal storage to provide more flexible electricity generation.Matching output with pricesThe research also examined how electricity market conditions could influence the operation of nuclear plants equipped with thermal storage.Electricity prices vary throughout the day as demand and available generation change. Prices can fall when renewable energy production is high and rise when demand increases or renewable output declines.By storing heat during lower-price periods and releasing it when electricity becomes more valuable, nuclear plants could potentially improve the revenue earned from their generation.The researchers used thermodynamic modeling to examine the proposed system’s operation and an economic optimization approach to assess how it could respond to changing market conditions.Their analysis included a rolling-horizon approach, which evaluates operating decisions over successive time periods rather than assuming a fixed schedule.However, the research remains a modeling study. The team has not demonstrated the integrated system at an operating nuclear power plant.The university’s announcement also did not provide specific figures for efficiency improvements, additional revenue, or the cost of installing thermal storage.Further engineering and economic assessments would be needed to establish whether the proposed approach could be commercially practical.The study was published in the Journal of Energy Resources Technology, Part A: Sustainable and Renewable Energy.
