title: Artificial channels separate lithium up to five times more selectively
content: Researchers in the US have developed artificial channels that are up to five times more selective for lithium than other recently developed lithium transporters, potentially offering a simpler way to extract the critical battery material.The nanoscale channels, developed at the University of Texas at Austin, allow lithium ions to pass through while restricting competing elements commonly found alongside them. The researchers say the channels are among the most selective developed so far.The technology takes inspiration from biological channels that control the movement of ions and molecules across living cell membranes. By recreating this function in artificial structures, the team aims to separate lithium without relying on conventional extraction methods that can consume substantial energy and produce chemical waste.Lithium is essential for batteries used in electric vehicles, smartphones and energy storage systems. However, extracting it from underground brines, hard rock and recycled batteries remains challenging because it is often mixed with sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium.Tiny channels filter lithiumThe researchers developed nanoscale pores designed to favor the movement of lithium ions over other dissolved substances.The channels use two features to achieve this separation: chemical groups positioned near their entrances and a confined internal structure that influences how ions move through them.As ions approach the opening, they interact with the chemical groups. These interactions, combined with the restricted space inside the channel, help determine which ions can pass through more easily.In laboratory experiments, the artificial channels demonstrated lithium selectivity two to five times higher than other recently developed lithium transporters, according to the researchers.The findings build on the team’s earlier work developing similar technology to separate rare earth elements used in industrial applications.Manish Kumar, a professor of civil, architectural and environmental engineering and chemical engineering at UT Austin, said the goal is to simplify the recovery of lithium from complex mixtures.“Our goal is a process that is faster, cleaner and easier to run,” Kumar said.The researchers believe the approach could eventually reduce the need for harsh solvents in lithium separation. However, the current results demonstrate selective ion transport rather than a complete industrial extraction process.Scaling membranes for extractionThe next challenge is incorporating the channels into larger membranes capable of processing significant quantities of lithium-containing solutions.The team is exploring a previously developed membrane material made from interconnected, cell-like layers. These structures can be assembled using lipids or polymer materials and could provide a framework for integrating the selective channels.The researchers envision a continuous separation system in which lithium-rich solutions pass through membranes that preferentially transport lithium ions.Such a process could potentially improve lithium recovery from underground brines while reducing the chemical demands of conventional separation methods.However, further testing is required to establish whether the channels can maintain their performance when exposed to real brines containing multiple dissolved salts.The researchers also need to determine how effectively the technology can operate at industrial scale. The announcement did not provide commercial-scale recovery rates, energy consumption figures, or operating costs.Beyond mining, the team sees possible applications in recovering lithium from spent batteries and developing improved separators for future battery designs.The research was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.

title: Autonomous pilot assistant flies three Pegasus tankers in world first
content: An AI-powered cockpit assistant has completed five flights aboard three operational U.S. Air Force tanker aircraft, testing how software can support pilots without controlling the aircraft. Beacon AI’s Murdock system logged approximately 20 hours aboard KC-46A Pegasus tankers during August and September 2026.The demonstrations took place under an Air Force AFWERX Tactical Funding Increase (TACFI) agreement with Air Mobility Command (AMC). Flights began during Emerald Flag at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida before continuing at two other airfields, including a civilian airport.Beacon says Murdock is the first commercially developed AI pilot assistant to fly aboard multiple operational aircraft. Its approach centers on processing flight data and providing recommendations through an onboard interface.Inside Murdock’s techMurdock combines onboard computing hardware with a crew-facing interface. It reads data from certified avionics buses, gives pilots advisory information, and records flight data for analysis.The system also connects to Lighthouse, Beacon’s cloud-based fleet data platform, through satellite communications. Lighthouse processes information gathered across flights, helping Beacon develop software features aimed at improving safety and operational efficiency.This architecture lets the company develop cockpit assistance without replacing existing avionics or modifying certified flight-critical systems. Pilots retain control and responsibility for operational decisions.Beacon classifies the demonstrated capability as Level 2 assistance within its own framework. The software advises the crew, but humans decide how to respond.CEO Matt Cox said the flights demonstrate how the technology can deliver practical benefits to aircrews. He added that Beacon plans to expand its capabilities as operational experience and supporting evidence accumulate.Fleet data drives upgradesFlying aboard operational tankers gives Beacon access to real-world data from different aircraft and operating environments. The flights covered multiple airfields and procedures, offering a broader range of conditions than a single-aircraft demonstration.Beacon calls its longer-term approach Fleet Learning. The concept uses accumulated flight data to refine software features across participating aircraft, potentially helping operators benefit from improvements developed through shared operational experience.AFWERX backed the project through its TACFI program, which helps advance technologies toward operational use. The agreement followed a Small Business Innovation Research Phase 2 contract with U.S. Special Operations Command.The effort also reflects growing defense interest in software that improves cockpit awareness without taking control away from pilots. The House Armed Services Committee addressed advisory flight-assistance systems in its report on the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act.Lawmakers directed the defense secretary to brief the committee by February 1, 2027, on plans to evaluate and adopt these technologies.Beyond military aircraftThe KC-46 could offer Beacon a route toward commercial aviation. The tanker derives from Boeing’s 767 platform, which has recorded 1,361 deliveries since 1982.However, military demonstrations do not establish readiness or regulatory approval for commercial passenger aircraft. Any expansion would require further development, testing, and validation.Beacon’s immediate goal is to extend Murdock’s support across more stages of flight. Planned capabilities include assistance with mission scheduling and postflight debriefing.The broader engineering challenge is to make cockpit software more useful through repeated operational testing. Its success will depend on whether data-driven improvements reduce crew workload and support safer decisions without disrupting established flight procedures.

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in Cancer Cells That Could Transform Treatment
content:
Cell experiments revealed that the cancer drug target Wee1 also helps healthy cells copy DNA, a previously overlooked role that could explain treatment toxicity and guide safer therapies. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals a previously overlooked weakness in certain cancer cells that could help researchers refine targeted treatments and reduce harmful side effects.
Cancer cells that have lost one safeguard against DNA damage can become dependent on another, an enzyme called Wee1. Drugs that block Wee1 aim to exploit that weakness, but serious side effects are disrupting clinical trials and threatening their adoption in the clinic.
One of the cell’s main safeguards is the tumor-suppressor protein p53, which can halt the cell cycle when DNA damage is detected. In around half of all cancers, p53 is inactive, allowing damaged cells to continue growing. Wee1 provides a second line of defense, acting as a backup brake that prevents cells with damaged DNA from entering cell division. Cancers with mutated p53 rely on this remaining safeguard, making Wee1 an attractive drug target.
Blocking Wee1 may stall healthy cells
A study published in
has now revealed that Wee1 also helps healthy cells begin copying their DNA, much earlier in the cell cycle. Researchers from the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS), the University of Oxford, and UCL found that this role involves a protein degradation complex, a group of proteins that breaks down molecules needed for DNA replication. Wee1 helps switch off the complex so replication can begin. Without Wee1, the complex remains active, delaying or preventing cells from progressing through the cell cycle.
“We think what’s happening in patients is that when they’re being treated with these Wee1 inhibitors, it’s stopping their normal fast proliferating cells, like you get in the colon and the blood system, from starting to replicate,” says Alexis, head of the Cell Cycle Control group at the LMS. “And so those cells are stuck, unable to generate new cells, and that could be causing some of the toxic side effects.”
Cell experiments challenge the Wee1 model
The discovery grew out of an effort to test the established understanding of Wee1’s activity early in the cell cycle. The team built a mathematical model based on the scientific literature to predict what would happen when the enzyme was inhibited.
“Wee1 has been very intensely studied in the later stages of the cell cycle, where targeting its activity for cancer treatment makes sense,” says Alexis. “However, the side effects of Wee1 inhibitors in patients were hard to explain based on these functions so we started to wonder if this Wee1 enzyme had some other function that we hadn’t appreciated that could explain these. We wanted to look earlier in the cell cycle to see if there was something we had missed.”
Human epithelial cells labelled for a Wee1 target (phosphorylated CDK; in yellow) and DNA (in blue). Credit: Cell Cycle Control Group, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences
The researchers then tested the model’s predictions in healthy and cancerous cells. Alexis says, “We quickly found out that the model we had based on the literature on Wee1 was wrong because that was not what we saw in cells. What had been missed was an early function of Wee1 that people hadn’t looked at.”
Matching Wee1 inhibitors to vulnerable cancers
If the side effects are linked to Wee1’s role in controlling the protein degradation complex, the findings could help identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment. The researchers suggest that cancers with reduced activity of this complex may be particularly susceptible to Wee1 inhibitors. That could create a therapeutic window in which lower doses kill cancer cells while limiting damage to healthy cells and reducing side effects.
“We’re also starting to think about if there are different ways we could inhibit Wee1 that get round this early cell cycle function,” says Alexis, “though how this might be achieved is a work in progress.”
The researchers now want to test the work’s predictions further in preclinical models and in patients currently enrolled in Wee1 inhibitor clinical trials. Those tests could help determine whether the newly identified function explains the toxic effects and how that understanding might guide safer treatment.
“Now we’ve uncovered this new function for Wee1, are there other functions that we haven’t appreciated? What else is it doing that we have not seen since we’ve not looked at the right stage?” asks Alexis.
Reference: “WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry” by Luc-Alban Vuillemenot, Lucas G. Morales, Calin-Mihai Dragoi, Betheney R. Pennycook, Edward Harris, Liuyang C. Lin, William A. Weston, Jade-Ellen Brown, Emma Graham, Leelou Moulin, Ivan Andrew, Georgia Roumelioti, Alex Montoya, Laurence Game, George R. Young, Keshava K. Datta, Pavel Shliaha, Béla Novák, Hiroyuki Yamano and Alexis R. Barr, 21 October 2026,

title: Obesity Could Disable a Key Defense Against Breast Cancer, Study Finds
content:
Scientists have discovered that fat cells in breast tissue may play an unexpected role in protecting against cancer. Credit: Shutterstock
A hopeful new direction in the fight against breast cancer may lie in the body’s own defenses, as mouse experiments suggest that protection weakened by obesity could be restored.
Breast cancer develops in tissue surrounded by fat cells, and those cells may play a greater role in controlling tumor growth than previously understood. Researchers have discovered that fat cells in lean breast tissue produce a molecule that helps destroy cancerous cells. In obesity, production of this protective molecule drops, potentially removing one of the body’s natural defenses against breast cancer.
The finding comes from researchers at Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah (the U), who identified a previously underappreciated way obesity may contribute to breast cancer. Rather than simply creating conditions that encourage cancer growth, obesity may also weaken a biological process that normally helps eliminate dangerous cells.
The research was led by Keren Hilgendorf, PhD, a Huntsman Cancer Institute investigator and assistant professor of biochemistry at the U, and first author Meghan Curtin, a doctoral candidate in molecular biology at the university. Their findings were published in the journal
Keren Hilgendorf, PhD. Credit: Huntsman Cancer Institute
Lean fat cells promote cancer cell death
Much of the breast consists of fat cells called adipocytes. These cells become larger with obesity, changing the surrounding tissue environment in ways that can affect cancer cells. By studying preclinical models, including breast tissue from donors, the researchers identified a key difference between lean and obese adipocytes involving a fatty acid known as 9S-HODE.
Lean adipocytes produced substantially more 9S-HODE than obese adipocytes. This molecule helps promote ferroptosis, a form of cell death involving iron-dependent damage to cellular fats. Ferroptosis is one of the processes through which the body can eliminate old or damaged cells, including those that could become cancerous.
“We found that the lean adipocytes produce much more 9S-HODE than obese ones. This means that cancerous cells die more readily in lean tissue,” says Curtin. “By producing more 9S-HODE, our bodies are actively protecting us, under lean circumstances, in a way it cannot with obesity.”
Boosting 9S-HODE suppresses tumor growth in mice
The researchers also tested whether restoring this molecule could change tumor growth. In preclinical mouse models, increasing 9S-HODE levels in obese adipocytes suppressed breast cancer tumor growth. This suggests that the reduced production of 9S-HODE associated with obesity may contribute directly to the loss of a protective mechanism.
For Hilgendorf, the results offer a different way to understand the relationship between obesity and cancer.
“We uncovered the role of a molecule that normally appears in lean tissue that restrains breast cancer growth but is less present with obesity,” says Hilgendorf. “We know obesity is often a driver of breast cancer, and researchers in our field usually consider how obesity is promoting the disease. But we hadn’t really considered that obesity could also be the loss of something that naturally protects us.”
Meghan Curtin, Doctoral Candidate. Credit: Huntsman Cancer Institute
Could 9S-HODE become a cancer therapy?
That distinction could have implications for treatment. If 9S-HODE helps limit tumor growth, researchers may eventually be able to develop therapies that restore its protective activity. The mouse experiments provide early evidence supporting this possibility, although further research is needed to determine whether the approach could work in patients.
“From a clinical perspective, this discovery is incredibly empowering. Because 9S-HODE is naturally present in the body but is lost with obesity, we may be able to restore this protection by putting it back,” says Hilgendorf. “That could become a very feasible therapeutic approach to slow breast cancer growth.”
The researchers emphasize that obesity is only one of several factors contributing to breast cancer, which can also develop for unrelated reasons. Their findings suggest that 9S-HODE is produced primarily by fat cells in the breast, although fat cells elsewhere in the body may provide similar protection. Whether this mechanism operates in other tissues remains an open question.
“We believe this shift in the understanding of the roles of lean and obese adipocytes is the start of something. This is just one discovery, and it’s not the end of the road,” says Curtin. “This opened our eyes to new ways to think about science, and hopefully we can harness what our bodies are already doing to make progress against this disease.”
Reference: “Lean adipocyte oxylipin signaling restrains breast cancer through ferroptosis” by Meghan C. Curtin, Abigail E. Jackson, Mark D. Lee, Elisabeth A. Brown, J. Alan Maschek, David H. Lum, James E. Cox, Alana L. Welm and Keren I. Hilgendorf, 10 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1126/science.aea4287

title: Ultra-Processed Foods May Be Changing How Children’s Brains Respond to Food
content:
Scientists have uncovered a potential connection between ultra-processed diets, the brain’s reward system, and changes in children’s body composition. Credit: Shutterstock
A yearlong study of 46 children suggests that brain responses to tempting food images may partly explain the link between ultra-processed diets and increasing body fat.
Ultra-processed foods account for about
67% of the daily calories
consumed by children in the United States. Although these products have been linked to weight gain and other health problems, scientists are still trying to understand how they may interact with the developing brain. New research suggests that children who eat more ultra-processed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing food images, and those responses are associated with increases in body fat one year later.
Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) include products such as certain breakfast cereals, packaged breads, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and shelf-stable, often containing artificial sweeteners, colors, and other ingredients not typically used in home cooking. Previous studies have linked UPF consumption to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, but the role of the brain’s reward system in these associations remains unclear.
Childhood may be an especially important time to investigate this relationship because the brain is still developing and food preferences are taking shape.
“Children’s brains are still developing, habits are still forming, and food preferences are still being made. It’s an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment,” said study senior author Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. “We’re particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference.”
Brain scans reveal stronger reward responses
To explore how UPF consumption relates to brain activity and weight gain, researchers studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the long-term
BrainChild study
, which investigates diabetes and obesity risk. All participants began at a healthy weight, allowing the team to examine potential early signs of increased risk.
At the beginning of the study, researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to monitor the children’s brain activity while they viewed pictures of appealing foods, including cookies and French fries. The team also collected information about each child’s diet, body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and waist circumference. BMI is a measurement based on height and weight. One year later, researchers measured BMI, body fat percentage, and waist circumference again.
The brain scans revealed that children who consumed more UPFs had stronger responses to food pictures in the dorsal striatum, a brain region involved in reward and motivation. Children with stronger responses in this region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the following year.
Brain responses may help explain weight gain
When they statistically accounted for how strongly each child’s dorsal striatum responded to food images, the association between UPF consumption and BMI weakened by 31%. The association with body fat percentage weakened by 44%. These findings suggest that the brain’s sensitivity to appealing food cues may help explain part of the relationship between UPF consumption and changes in body composition.
“This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain,” Page said. “It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time.”
The findings, published in
JAMA Network Open
, provide evidence of a possible connection between diet, reward-related brain activity, and subsequent changes in body fat. The research was funded in part by the National Institutes of Health.
Whether diet changes the brain remains unknown
However, because the study was observational, it cannot establish that eating UPFs directly changes brain activity or causes weight gain. The results also do not determine whether stronger brain responses lead children to consume more UPFs or whether their diets influence how the brain responds to food.
To investigate cause and effect, Page hopes to conduct an intervention study in which children who regularly consume UPFs are provided with more minimally processed foods. Researchers could then examine whether changing their diets alters their brain responses to food images over time and whether those changes are associated with less weight gain.
The researchers also emphasize that improving children’s diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed foods are often among the most affordable, convenient, and accessible options, making dietary changes difficult without broader improvements in food availability.
“Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution,” Page said.
Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue following participants through puberty and into young adulthood. By tracking changes in brain activity, body composition, diet, and overall health, researchers hope to better understand how eating habits during childhood relate to health later in life.
Reference: “Ultraprocessed Food Intake, Striatal Response to Food Cues, and Adiposity Gain in Children” by Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, Jared Smith, Ting Chow, Kay Jann, Anny H. Xiang and Kathleen A. Page, ,
JAMA Network Open
DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.40252
This research was supported by an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36]; the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. The REDCap database used for this study was supported by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].

title: Hubble Finds a Stunning Twist in How the Universe Emerged From Darkness
content:
This painting shows massive stars emitting ionizing radiation, but gas swept up by supernova-driven galactic winds can prevent that radiation from escaping the galaxy. Credit: Siyi Wang
Hubble observations of nearby starburst galaxies challenge the idea that supernova winds helped reionize the early universe, suggesting young stars may have enabled radiation to escape before those winds formed.
Powerful winds from exploding stars were thought to clear paths for ultraviolet radiation to escape early galaxies. A new study of nearby galaxies suggests those winds may instead make escape more difficult, challenging a leading explanation for how the universe emerged from a fog of neutral hydrogen.
Within the first billion years after the Big Bang, that fog made the universe opaque to ultraviolet light. It began to clear during an era called reionization, which started about 13 billion years ago. Energetic radiation from early galaxies struck neutral hydrogen atoms, separating them into charged protons and electrons.
“Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today,” said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Astronomy at the University of Michigan. “We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe.”
For radiation to transform the gas between galaxies, it first had to get out of the galaxies that produced it. Astronomers proposed that supernovae, or large exploding stars, helped by generating winds powerful enough to reshape galaxies and clear routes through the surrounding gas.
“Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn’t what we thought,” Carr said.
Faster winds, less escaping radiation
Carr led and carried out the study as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China before joining Michigan. The international team, which includes University of Michigan researchers, used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe nearby starburst galaxies, where stars form at exceptionally high rates. These galaxies resemble some of those thought to have helped reionize the early universe, giving researchers a way to investigate how radiation escapes.
The team analyzed the galaxies’ spectra, which separate their light into different wavelengths, to measure the speeds of their galactic winds. Gas moving in those winds absorbs light at specific wavelengths, leaving dips whose positions and widths reveal how the gas is moving. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.
“It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape,” said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.
Young stars may help radiation escape
The findings, published in
Nature Astronomy
, strengthen an alternative explanation centered on activity from young stars. Radiation and smaller winds operating in the neighborhoods of these stars could help light escape.
“Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form,” Carr said.
The researchers are working to secure more Hubble observing time to examine additional galaxies and further test the role of these smaller winds. Hubble is a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency. The telescope also supported the study through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.
Connecting the behavior of nearby galaxies to the universe’s early transformation remains an unfinished task. “We don’t know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved,” Carr said. “We know that it took place, but we don’t have complete answers to those questions.”
The observations can already inform computer simulations that astronomers use to investigate reionization, particularly how stellar activity changes the gas through which radiation must travel.
“Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies,” said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. “Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode.”

title: This Giant Planet Orbits Its Star Every Two Days – but Something Is Very Wrong
content:
After around 2033, planet TOI-1355 b will disappear from view as it must pass between the star and Earth to be seen. There would be no major changes for the planet itself. But astronomers will become unable to observe its transits to characterize the planetary nature for hundreds of years. © ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann CC-BY Credit: ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann CC-BY
Astronomers have discovered an unusual planet with an extremely hot host star and a highly eccentric orbit that challenges expectations for its class.
A giant planet racing around an unusually hot star has caught astronomers’ attention because of its highly elongated orbit. Known as TOI-1355 b, the planet completes one revolution in roughly two Earth days, following a path that differs sharply from the nearly circular orbits typical of many hot Jupiters.
Researchers from the
University of Tokyo
and their international collaborators believe the planet’s unusual trajectory could help explain how giant planets migrate toward their stars. However, its changing orbit is expected to limit observations after approximately 2033, leaving scientists a relatively short window to investigate its behavior.
An Unusual Orbit Around an Extremely Hot Star
TOI-1355 b belongs to a class of exoplanets called hot Jupiters, massive gas giants that orbit exceptionally close to their host stars. Its star, TOI-1355, has a surface temperature of approximately 8,400 degrees Celsius (15,152 degrees Fahrenheit), compared with about 5,500 degrees Celsius (9,932 degrees Fahrenheit) for the Sun.
Although astronomers have discovered thousands of planets around stars similar to or cooler than the Sun, planetary systems surrounding hotter stars remain less thoroughly explored. Project Researcher Noriharu Watanabe and Professor Norio Narita of the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences are investigating these systems to better understand the diversity of planets beyond our solar system.
“Planet surveys around stars as hot or cooler than the sun are flourishing, and thousands of planets have been discovered around such stars. But planet surveys around hotter stars are still not advanced,” said Watanabe. “In this project, we hunted for planets around hot stars to examine the diversity of exoplanets more broadly. When we investigated the change in brightness of TOI-1355 from prior data, we found that the secondary eclipse, a phenomenon in which a planet passes behind a star, occurred faster than the timing assumed for a circular orbit. This was unusual for hot Jupiters around hot stars, and this is why we began to research this planet in detail.”
How Changes in Starlight Exposed the Planet’s Orbit
NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) first detected periodic decreases in TOI-1355’s brightness. Narita’s team identified these dips as planetary transits, which occur when a planet passes in front of its star from Earth’s perspective and temporarily blocks a small fraction of its light.
The researchers also examined the secondary eclipse, when the planet passes behind its star. Its unexpected timing indicated that TOI-1355 b was traveling along an elliptical rather than circular orbit. By analyzing brightness variations recorded by TESS, the team determined the planet’s mass and orbital eccentricity, a measurement of how far an orbit deviates from a perfect circle. Calculating the mass required more complex mathematical models to account for the planet’s elongated trajectory.
Clues to a Planet’s Turbulent History
One possible explanation for TOI-1355 b’s orbit involves gravitational encounters with other massive planets or celestial bodies. Such interactions can dramatically alter a planet’s trajectory, sending it into a highly eccentric orbit. Over time, tidal forces from the host star can shrink and gradually circularize that orbit, potentially producing the close, nearly circular paths observed in many hot Jupiters.
“It is considered that the planetary orbit had become highly elliptical, initially due to the gravitational interaction with other celestial bodies, such as other giant planets, and shrunk gradually later due to the tidal effect of its host star,” said Watanabe.
The discovery supports theoretical predictions that hot Jupiters around hotter stars may undergo dramatic orbital migration. Researchers have not established which interactions shaped TOI-1355 b’s particular orbit, but its pronounced eccentricity is consistent with a history of gravitational disturbances followed by tidal evolution.
The team is now investigating how the planet’s orbital plane is tilted relative to the star’s rotation, another measurement that could help reconstruct its past. The researchers are preparing a separate paper on this work and planning an observation proposal involving NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. With the planet’s evolving orbit expected to prevent the same transit and eclipse observations after around 2033, the opportunity to collect these measurements is limited.
Reference: “Discovery of an eccentric hot super-jupiter leaving the transiting geometry of the early-A-type star TOI-1355” by Noriharu Watanabe, Norio Narita, Akihiko Fukui, Bun’ei Sato, Keisuke Isogai, John H Livingston, Jerome P de Leon, Daniel Huber, Yugo Kawai, Yuya Hayashi, Masashi Omiya, Hideyuki Izumiura, Akito Tajitsu, Keivan G Stassun, Eric Girardin, Giuseppe Marino, Antonio Frasca, Giovanni Catanzaro, Javier Alonso-Santiago, Manfred Raetz, Stephanie Striegel, Nobuhiko Kusakabe and Motohide Tamura, 18 September 2026,

title: This Alien Planet Should Have Lost Its Atmosphere Billions of Years Ago
content:
Artist’s concept of the lava world TOI-561 b and its star, whose surface churns with hot, bubbling gas. Webb observations show the planet reflects most of its starlight, and models suggest bright silicate clouds above its magma ocean may be the reason. Credit: CryoDragon Inc
James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that exotic mineral clouds may be shielding a distant lava planet from its star.
A rocky planet exposed to extreme heat from its star appears to reflect nearly three-quarters of the starlight that reaches it. Astronomers suspect silicate-mineral clouds could act as a protective sunscreen, helping the planet maintain temperatures far below those expected for an exposed surface of molten rock.
The planet, TOI-561 b, lies about 280 light-years from Earth and was previously considered too hot to retain a substantial atmosphere. New observations from the
James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)
suggest that it has a significant envelope of gas that reflects incoming radiation and redistributes heat around the planet. The findings, published in
The Astronomical Journal
, challenge existing theories about how atmospheres survive on intensely irradiated rocky worlds.
Webb Observations Reveal an Unusual Temperature Pattern
An international research team, including University of Birmingham astrophysicist Dr. Anjali Piette, monitored TOI-561 b for 37 hours, covering nearly four complete orbits around its star. By measuring changes in the planet’s brightness and thermal emission throughout its orbit, the researchers investigated how heat is distributed between its permanently illuminated dayside and its dark nightside.
Earlier observations had shown that the dayside was unexpectedly cool for a bare, dark rocky surface. Scientists considered whether winds might be transporting the missing heat to the nightside or whether the planet was reflecting much of the incoming starlight. Webb’s first measurements of the nightside showed that it was not warm enough to account for the difference. The results indicate that TOI-561 b reflects approximately 75% of the starlight it receives, a proportion comparable to Venus.
Professor Lisa Dang, the project’s lead researcher at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, explained: “We measured how the planet’s brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere.”
Could Clouds Made of Rock Protect the Planet?
To investigate the planet’s unusual reflectivity, the researchers compared their measurements with computer simulations of its climate. The models suggest that clouds containing silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium silicate (MgSiO3), could form on the dayside. These clouds might reflect substantial amounts of stellar radiation before it can heat the surface, much as a sunscreen reduces the amount of sunlight absorbed by skin.
The atmosphere’s chemical composition remains unknown. One possibility is a dense layer of carbon dioxide, resembling the atmosphere of Venus but exposed to much more extreme conditions. Another is an atmosphere rich in sulfur dioxide, a volcanic gas also released by Jupiter’s moon Io. Neither scenario would produce habitable conditions.
Why Hasn’t the Atmosphere Disappeared?
The evidence for a substantial atmosphere raises questions about the planet’s history. Intense stellar radiation should have stripped much of the gas from a rocky world like TOI-561 b over billions of years. Yet the new measurements strengthen
earlier findings
suggesting that the planet still possesses a thick atmosphere, potentially replenished by gases escaping from its molten interior.
Dr. Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said: “Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.”
“Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface, acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere.”
The Next Question: What Is the Atmosphere Made Of?
Determining which gases surround TOI-561 b could help researchers understand how its atmosphere has persisted under such extreme conditions. Additional Webb observations at longer wavelengths may provide the spectral information needed to distinguish between competing atmospheric models and investigate whether volcanic activity is continually replacing gases lost to space.
Professor Dang added: “The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b’s atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of Io. Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years.”
Reference: “A Highly Reflective Atmosphere on the Lava World TOI-561b Revealed by JWST/NIRSpec Phase Curves” by Samuel Boucher, Lisa Dang, Alex McGinty, Johanna K. Teske, Raymond Pierrehumbert, Anjali A. A. Piette, Nicole L. Wallack, Angharad Weeks, Neil T. Lewis, Tim Lichtenberg, Mykhaylo Plotnykov, Emma Postolec, Daniel Huber, Timothy R. Bedding, Harrison Nicholls, Bo Peng, Mark Hammond and Diana Valencia, 29 September 2026,
The Astronomical Journal

title: Beyond Bad Cholesterol: Scientists Uncover a Hidden Driver of Heart Disease
content:
Researchers have uncovered unexpected molecular similarities between two types of blood lipoproteins, pointing to inflammatory pathways that could reshape heart disease prevention. Credit: Shutterstock
Protein patterns linked to TRL and Lp(a), two types of fat-carrying particles, suggest shared inflammatory pathways that could offer new targets for heart disease prevention.
Lowering “bad” cholesterol substantially reduces the risk of a heart attack, yet some people still develop coronary heart disease after treatment brings their LDL cholesterol down to a recommended level. Other particles that carry fats through the blood can contribute to the risk that remains. Understanding how they affect blood vessels could help researchers find more precise ways to prevent heart disease.
Coronary heart disease develops when cholesterol accumulates in the blood vessels supplying the heart and can lead to a heart attack if untreated. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes accounting for more than four out of five of those deaths.
Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden measured almost 3,000 proteins in blood samples from around 35,000 UK Biobank participants without previous heart disease, to see if differences in blood proteins could give any clues as to why a risk of heart disease still prevails in some people after bad cholesterol levels are brought down to a healthy level. Credit: Wikimedia Commons
Cholesterol carriers are not equally harmful
Researchers at
Chalmers University of Technology
in Sweden have now identified blood protein patterns that offer clues to what happens beyond cholesterol buildup. Two types of fat-carrying particles, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRL) and lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), shared many protein patterns and signs of potentially harmful biological effects. The pattern associated with LDL, or low-density lipoprotein, was mainly linked to cholesterol accumulating in artery walls.
All three types of particles can deposit cholesterol in artery walls, and LDL is the most abundant. But abundance does not tell the whole story. A
previous study
Clemens Wittenbecher, Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics, at the Department of Life Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden. Credit: Chalmers University of Technology | Martina Butorac
“For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs,” says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology.
Protein patterns point to shared inflammation
The team used proteomics, the study of proteins, to examine how the three types of particles affect the body. Proteins carry out essential functions, and their levels can change with diet, stress, aging, or disease. Measuring them provides a snapshot of how the body is functioning at that moment. The researchers combined measurements of almost 3,000 blood proteins with genetic data and long-term health records to identify patterns that might help explain how the particles damage arteries.
The overlapping protein patterns associated with TRL and Lp(a) appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease. These particles also contained proteins that attract immune cells, which could contribute to inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. Although TRL and Lp(a) are different types of particles, the findings suggested that some of their harmful effects may involve shared biological pathways.
A graphic showing three types of fat-carrying particles (lipoproteins) which can deposit cholesterol in the blood vessel walls. Their common feature is apolipoprotein B particle on their surface. Credit: Chalmers University of Technology | Jakub Morze
“The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings,” says Morze. “It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.”
“Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention,” says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. “Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.”

title: Drinking Tea May Lower Your Risk of Vascular Disease – but There’s a Catch
content:
Tea is one of the world’s most widely consumed beverages, enjoyed for its diverse flavors and potential health benefits. Rich in natural compounds such as polyphenols and antioxidants, tea has attracted scientific interest for its possible effects on heart health, metabolism, and overall well-being. Credit: Shutterstock
Not all tea-drinking habits were associated with the same health benefits. Researchers found that tea type, strength, and temperature were linked to notable differences in vascular disease risk.
People who regularly drank tea had a lower risk of diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels in a large study in China. However, the pattern varied with the type, strength, and temperature of the tea, with “burning hot” tea associated with elevated risk.
The study, published in the
Journal of Internal Medicine
, followed 485,934 adults for a median of 9.05 years. Researchers recorded 14,863 cases of cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, pulmonary heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. These conditions involve the heart and circulation, including blood vessels in the brain, heart problems related to lung disease, and reduced blood flow through arteries supplying the limbs. Regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of these outcomes compared with not drinking tea.
Tea drinking was also considered alongside smoking and physical activity, providing context for how it fit into a broader pattern of habits.
“Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status, and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk,” the authors wrote.
Tea type, strength, and temperature matter
Among weekly tea drinkers, the lowest risk was estimated at approximately 6 to 8 cups per day. Black tea showed more consistent associations with lower vascular disease risk than green tea, while moderate-strength tea was associated with the lowest risk. These findings describe associations, rather than establishing that a particular amount or preparation of tea prevents disease.
The elevated risk associated with “burning hot” tea contrasts with the lower risk linked to regular tea consumption overall. Temperature therefore matters when interpreting the findings, but the reported results do not explain why very hot tea was associated with higher risk or establish that heat itself caused the increase.

Journal of Internal Medicine

title: A Routine Blood Test Could Predict Dementia Risk 15 Years in Advance
content:
A routine blood test measuring hemoglobin levels may offer clues about a person’s risk of developing dementia up to 15 years later, according to a large study. Credit: Shutterstock
A large study tracking more than 316,000 adults for up to 15 years suggests that a routine blood test may reveal important clues about future dementia risk.
A standard blood test taken during a routine health check could offer clues about dementia risk more than a decade later. In a study of more than 316,000 adults, researchers found that people with unusually low or high levels of hemoglobin were more likely to develop dementia, although the risks varied depending on the type of disease.
Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. Low levels are commonly associated with anemia, while unusually high levels can result from smoking, dehydration, or certain heart and lung conditions. The findings suggest that this familiar blood measurement may also reflect broader aspects of physical health associated with brain aging.
Tracking Dementia Risk for Up to 15 Years
Researchers analyzed health records from 316,542 Korean adults aged 40 and older who underwent national health screenings in 2004 and 2005. Participants were divided into five groups based on their hemoglobin levels, from the lowest 20% to the highest 20%. National health insurance records were then used to track new dementia diagnoses through the end of 2019.
Compared with the group that had the lowest dementia rate, participants in the lowest hemoglobin category had a 16% higher risk of developing dementia from any cause. Those in the highest category had a 7% greater risk.
The findings, published in the
Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease
and presented at the 39th ECNP Congress in Munich, also identified differences between Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia.
Alzheimer’s and Vascular Dementia Show Different Patterns
For Alzheimer’s disease, the increased risk was concentrated among people with the lowest hemoglobin levels. Participants in this group were 14% more likely to develop the disease than those in the reference group.
The relationship was different for vascular dementia (caused by reduced blood flow to the brain). People in the lowest hemoglobin category had a 19% higher risk, while those in the highest category had an 18% higher risk. However, the association did not follow a consistent pattern across all five hemoglobin groups. The researchers also observed clearer and more consistent relationships among women than men.
What Hemoglobin Levels May Reveal About Brain Health
Lead researcher Dr. Hyun Soo Kim, an assistant professor at Dong-A University College of Medicine in Busan, South Korea, emphasized that the results do not establish a direct causal relationship.
“The findings do not show that hemoglobin itself causes dementia, but suggest that abnormal hemoglobin levels may be a visible marker of wider physical vulnerability relevant to brain health.”
Kim added, “Dementia is one of the fastest-growing health challenges in aging societies, and there are not many treatments and no cure. Identifying simple, accessible markers of future risk could help researchers and clinicians better understand how whole-body health relates to brain health over time.”
Could Routine Blood Tests Help Identify Future Risk?
Hemoglobin is already measured in standard blood tests around the world, making it considerably more accessible than specialized brain imaging or newer dementia biomarkers. The researchers suggest that existing blood test results could potentially help scientists investigate connections between general physical health and long-term cognitive decline.
Kim explained, “A blood test most people already get at a routine check-up may say something about their brain health many years later. In this large Korean cohort, people with unusually low hemoglobin, and, to a smaller degree, those with unusually high hemoglobin, were more likely to develop dementia. This does not prove that hemoglobin causes dementia, but it supports the idea that general physical health, including the body’s ability to carry oxygen, matters for long-term brain health.”
Why the Findings Do Not Prove Cause and Effect
Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether abnormal hemoglobin levels contribute directly to dementia. Other medical conditions could influence both hemoglobin measurements and brain health. Early dementia processes might also affect nutrition, body weight, frailty, or anemia before the disease is formally diagnosed.
“We want to emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as advice to take iron supplements, to raise hemoglobin levels, or to lower high hemoglobin levels in order to prevent dementia. An abnormal hemoglobin result should instead be discussed with a doctor, because it may point to underlying health issues that deserve attention,” Kim said.
More Research Is Needed Across Different Populations
The study drew on health records from South Korea, leaving questions about whether the same relationships apply to people from other ethnic, geographic, and medical backgrounds. Further research is also needed to establish whether identifying abnormal hemoglobin levels can meaningfully improve dementia risk assessment or prevention.
Dr. Lindsey Sinclair (University of Southampton), who was not involved in the research, commented:
“There is a growing body of evidence that physical health and brain health are intertwined. We are also increasingly aware that changes supporting better brain health, be they medical or lifestyle changes, are important in mid-life to reduce the risk of later dementia. While this study shows a possible link between hemoglobin levels and dementia risk, more work is required to understand if this link is present in people from a wider range of backgrounds; and what can best be done to reduce dementia risk in people with the lowest and highest levels of hemoglobin.”
Meeting: 39th ECNP Congress

title: A New Chemistry Breakthrough Could Change How Scientists Build Quantum Computers
content:
Chemistry
Diamond is one of the materials currently being investigated to make quantum computers and sensors. When nitrogen is added to diamond in a very specific way, the material has certain properties that could be ideal for quantum computers and sensors. Such diamond typically looks pink. Credit: Michael Livingston / PPPL Communications Department
Most materials being considered for quantum technology can hold a stable quantum state only when chilled to extreme temperatures. Diamond-based materials can work at room temperature, but their usefulness depends on defects in the crystal that have been difficult and computationally demanding to simulate.
At the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), staff research scientist Mark Martirez has developed a far faster way to calculate how those defects respond to light and microwave pulses. The approach has identified promising boron- and oxygen-based defects that could serve as qubits, the basic information-processing units of quantum computers and sensors. The research was recently published in
ACS Central Science
and has already attracted
attention
Diamond’s flaws can store quantum information
Pure diamond consists entirely of carbon atoms, but storing and processing quantum information requires a disruption in that structure. A carbon atom might be missing from its usual position, an atom of another element might take its place, or both changes might occur together. The cluster of atoms closest to the defect forms the qubit.
Scientists use laser light and microwave pulses to read information stored in these qubits. Most quantum diamond research has focused on the nitrogen-vacancy defect, in which a nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom and a nearby position normally occupied by another carbon atom is empty. When illuminated by a laser, this qubit emits red light if it is in a particular quantum state. Calculating how other defects respond to light and microwaves helps researchers assess whether they, too, could be useful.
Molecular models identify new qubit candidates
Martirez simplifies those calculations by computationally “carving out” a cluster of just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect and considering it in isolation. This makes highly accurate tools that chemists have used for decades to study simple compounds available for studying defects inside a solid.
“Because we’re treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule,” Martirez said. “This method really opened the floodgates” in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The calculations identified oxygen-based defects that shine blue and boron-based defects that emit ultraviolet light. These defects, known as color centers, could potentially serve different roles within a single quantum device.
“One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other,” Martirez said.
Chemistry’s path to custom qubits
Understanding the chemistry could also change how researchers conceive of a qubit’s structure. Diamond-based qubits are often treated as a physics problem, but Martirez’s work shows that chemistry offers another way to understand them. A fuller chemical understanding could let scientists design and build qubits for specific purposes, much as chemists design custom molecules, such as a new medication.
Martirez encouraged other chemists to bring their expertise into solid-state physics. “At this moment in time, there’s a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer,” he said. “But it’s not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.”
Practical quantum devices could eventually support sensors with greater sensitivity and accuracy than those currently available, along with computers capable of tackling highly complex problems far faster than today’s conventional supercomputers. Developing these future technologies is among the strategic national priorities PPPL works to advance.
For quantum chemistry, that progress could create a useful cycle. The field could help develop tools that allow it to “enrich itself” in the decades ahead, Martirez said. He expects a practical system containing multiple qubits to greatly improve the accuracy of quantum chemistry calculations.
“We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins, and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.”
Reference: “A Chemist’s Guide to Solid-State Qubits: Diamond Color Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules” by John Mark P. Martirez, July 27, 2026,
ACS Central Science
DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548
Funding for this research comes from PPPL’s Laboratory Directed Research and Development under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, as well as additional support from DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

title: The Ocean’s Mysterious “Snow” Could Be Hiding a Powerful Climate Secret
content:
Viscous marine snow particles (white) colonized by bacteria (orange) transport carbon to the deep ocean. Credit: Must credit Bryce Inman
A new imaging technique reveals how bacteria interact with the microscopic structure of marine snow.
A surprising property of the tiny particles sinking through the ocean could help determine how much carbon is stored in the deep sea. Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of marine snow affects how easily bacteria can break it down, potentially changing how much carbon reaches the ocean depths.
Researchers at UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln found that particularly gooey marine snow resists bacterial degradation. Their findings, published October 8 in
, suggest that highly viscous particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.
The Ocean’s Never-Ending Snowfall
Marine snow consists of tiny clumps of dead plankton, waste, mucus, minerals, and other debris that continuously descend through the water column. As these particles sink, they carry carbon from the sunlit surface ocean toward deeper waters, where some of it can remain stored for hundreds or thousands of years.
Scientists estimate that marine snow transports more than 10 gigatons (11 billion U.S. tons) of carbon away from the surface each year. However, only about 2 gigatons (2.2 billion U.S. tons) reach depths where the carbon can remain stored for extended periods. Much of the sinking material is broken down or recycled before reaching those depths.
The new research identifies particle viscosity, a measure of resistance to flow, as an important factor in this process. Marine snow particles vary in composition and consistency, and those differences influence how bacteria colonize and consume them.
Scientists Find a Way to See Inside Marine Snow
Understanding these interactions required a technique that had previously been unavailable: directly observing individual living bacteria as they navigate the microscopic structure of mucus.
“Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible,” said Bryce Inman, who began investigating the problem in 2021 while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Scripps Oceanography.
After four years of unsuccessful attempts, Inman and his colleagues, including Scripps microbiologist and professor emeritus Farooq Azam, developed a working approach in 2025. By combining 3D confocal microscopy with specialized fluorescent molecules, they could map the intricate physical structure of marine snow and track how bacteria interacted with it. The imaging technique is described in a companion study published in
Nature Communications
Why Stickier Marine Snow Carries More Carbon
The images showed that bacteria colonize less viscous regions near the surface of marine snow particles more easily than the thicker, more resistant material inside. These internal regions present a physical barrier that bacteria must gradually break down before penetrating farther into the particle.
“Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down,” Inman explained. “Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through”
Laboratory experiments confirmed that more viscous marine snow takes longer for bacteria to degrade and fragment. Computer simulations further suggested that these resistant particles can sink to greater depths before breaking apart. Together, the findings indicate that viscosity can substantially influence how much carbon escapes recycling in shallower waters and reaches the deep ocean.
What Ocean Slime Could Reveal About Other Ecosystems
The newly developed imaging method could also help researchers investigate interactions between bacteria and mucus in other environments. Similar relationships occur in coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive tracts of humans and other animals.
“Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, has a surprising amount of structure,” Inman said. “There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we’re really examining this physical habitat.”

title: Aging’s “Zombie Cell” Problem May Have a Solution, Scientists Discover
content:
Senescent cells, often called “zombie cells,” are cells that have stopped dividing but remain alive and metabolically active. Although they play important roles in wound healing and tissue repair, they can accumulate with age, releasing inflammatory substances that damage surrounding tissues and contribute to age-related diseases. Credit: Shutterstock
“Zombie cells” become harder to clear with age, and a new study reveals why the immune system struggles to remove them.
Researchers at Albert Einstein College of Medicine have identified a breakdown in protein recycling that helps explain why senescent cells, often called “zombie cells,” accumulate in aging tissues. In experiments involving older mice, restoring that process reduced senescent-cell buildup, inflammation, and tissue scarring. The findings, published in
Nature Aging
, suggest a possible way to help the immune system clear these cells more effectively.
Senescent cells remain alive after they stop dividing, but their activity changes. Although they can support tissue repair, their prolonged presence can fuel chronic inflammation and age-related disease. Most of the new experiments involved mice, with human lung samples providing evidence that the biological changes may also occur in people.
“In older animals, age-related changes in both senescent cells and the immune cells responsible for removing them allow these zombie cells to accumulate and play a role in disease,” said study leader Ana Maria Cuervo, M.D., Ph.D. “By restoring cellular recycling, we may be able to help the body’s own defenses clear these cells more effectively.”
Dr. Cuervo, study leader, distinguished professor of developmental & molecular biology and of medicine, and co-director of the Institute for Geroscience at Einstein. Credit: Albert Einstein College of Medicine
When Helpful Cells Overstay Their Welcome
Some injured cells enter senescence and release substances that recruit other cells to support repair. Once that work is done, immune cells called macrophages normally remove the senescent cells.
Macrophages also fight infection, dispose of dead cells, and regulate inflammation and tissue repair. The researchers found that their ability to remove senescent cells depends partly on chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), a recycling process that uses specialized “chaperone” molecules to select damaged or unnecessary proteins for breakdown.
When the team genetically altered mice so their macrophages lacked CMA, senescent cells lingered at wound sites, and healing slowed compared with control animals. The experiment showed how a defect inside immune cells can turn a temporary repair response into a lingering obstacle to recovery.
Cuervo, a leading CMA researcher, is a distinguished professor of developmental & molecular biology and medicine, the Robert and Renee Belfer Chair for the Study of Neurodegenerative Diseases, and co-director of Einstein’s Institute for Geroscience. Her
earlier research
established that CMA declines with age. Subsequent work linked
the resulting buildup of cellular waste
to Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases, as well as atherosclerosis and diabetes.
Old and Young Zombie Cells Behave Differently
The age-related decline in CMA also affects senescent cells themselves. To examine this, the researchers collected fibroblasts, cells found in connective tissue, from young and old mice. They then used drugs to stop the cells from dividing and induce senescence in the laboratory.
Cells from young mice responded by increasing CMA activity. Cells from old mice failed to increase their already low activity, allowing certain proteins to escape proper breakdown. They consequently released harmful substances that encouraged neighboring healthy cells to become senescent and interfered with macrophages’ ability to recognize and remove them.
At the same time, macrophages from older animals had lower CMA activity than those from younger animals and were less able to engulf senescent cells. Aging therefore disrupted both the cells awaiting removal and the immune cells responsible for clearing them.
Age-related changes in senescent cells could affect drug development. Researchers are developing senolytics to eliminate these cells, but testing them on cells taken from young animals and induced to become senescent in the lab may not accurately predict their effects in older bodies.
Restoring the Body’s Cleanup Process
The findings pointed toward another possibility: improve cellular recycling so senescent cells release fewer harmful substances and macrophages can recognize and engulf them more effectively. The team tested a compound it had previously developed, a small-molecule CMA activator called CA77.1.
Aged mice given CA77.1 orally every day for five months accumulated fewer senescent cells in several organs. They also showed fewer signs of inflammation and fibrosis, the buildup of scar tissue.
In a separate experiment, the researchers treated macrophages collected from aged mice with CA77.1. Their ability to engulf particles recovered to levels comparable to those of macrophages from young mice. That result demonstrated improved engulfing capacity, while the experiments in living animals showed reduced senescent-cell accumulation.
Testing A Link to Lung Fibrosis
The researchers next investigated idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), an aging-associated disease in which scar tissue progressively builds up in the lungs, making breathing increasingly difficult. People diagnosed with IPF have a median survival of three to five years.
Lung samples from patients with IPF showed markedly reduced CMA activity, prompting the researchers to test whether boosting it with CA77.1 could help in a mouse model of lung fibrosis. Treatment with CA77.1 soon after lung injury reduced scarring, senescence, and inflammation.
“Our research connects two major drivers of aging—declining CMA and cellular senescence—and shows for the first time how their interaction allows senescent cells to evade clearance by the immune system in old organisms,” said Dr. Cuervo. “We’ve also found that instead of trying to kill zombie cells, we may be able to restore their interaction with the immune system so that the body can clear them naturally. The next challenge is determining whether this approach can eventually be developed into a safe treatment for age-related diseases in people.”
Reference: “Decline of chaperone-mediated autophagy in aging impairs macrophage clearance of senescent cells” by Rebecca Sereda, Kristen Lindenau, Antonio Diaz, Zhaohui Liu, Olaya Santiago-Fernández, Rabia R. title: Unijet to launch an inkjet SAM coating tool for mass production of perovskite solar cells in February 2027
content:
Unijet to launch an inkjet SAM coating tool for mass production of perovskite solar cells in February 2027
, a South Korean maker of industrial inkjet equipment, plans to launch the TandemJet 4000 in February 2027, a mass-production tool that uses inkjet printing to coat self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) in solar cell manufacturing. The company is extending an ultrathin coating process previously validated in research and development and on a pilot system to mass production.
SAMs are ultrathin films that control interface properties between the layers of a solar cell. Unijet has developed an inkjet process that forms them at a thickness of 2-3 nanometers. The company has developed inks based on three SAM materials used at electrode interfaces in perovskite solar cells (MeO-4PACz, Me-4PACz and MeO-2PACz), as well as blended inks that combine two of the materials. It has achieved stable ink ejection at frequencies of up to 30 kHz.
Inkjet coating deposits the ink directly onto the designated areas, so no separate masks are needed. That makes patterns easier to change and reduces material consumption. Unijet is optimizing the process by evaluating how ink formulation and printing resolution affect film thickness and surface coverage.
The TandemJet 4000 is designed to process up to 4,000 wafers per hour, and to integrate pretreatment, ink printing, drying, heat treatment and inspection into a single production line. That is eight times the throughput of the company’s TandemJet 500 pilot system, which processes 500 wafers per hour. Unijet will also unveil a demonstration model of the TandemJet 2000, which is designed for 2,000 wafers per hour, at WCPEC-9 in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.
Unijet’s president, Kim Seok-soon, presented the company’s SAM inks, inkjet coating technology and equipment development at Perovskite Connect 2026 in Germany, on October 22.

title: Ricoh to build a production site for inkjet-printed perovskite solar cells, targeting several hundred MW by 2030
content:
Ricoh to build a production site for inkjet-printed perovskite solar cells, targeting several hundred MW by 2030
will establish manufacturing capabilities for inkjet-printed perovskite solar cells as it moves toward mass production. The company will build a production site at the Tohoku Site of Ricoh Industry in Shibata, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. It aims to reach annual production capacity of several hundred megawatts by 2030, with a future expansion to gigawatt-scale production.
The initiative has been selected for support under Japan’s GX (Green Transformation) Supply Chain Development Support Program, administered by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI). No funding amount has been disclosed.
Ricoh uses its inkjet technology to pattern-print all the functional layers of its perovskite solar cells. This lets it deposit the right amount of material exactly where it is needed, which the company says should improve material utilization, streamline manufacturing and reduce production costs. The company also draws on the organic photoconductor technology it developed for its multifunction printers, which it previously applied to organic solar cells.
Ricoh describes the work as part of its “Functional Printing” strategy, which applies the inkjet technology from its commercial and industrial printing businesses to the coating and deposition of functional materials.
The step follows Ricoh’s selection in September 2025 for
Japanese government funding to advance perovskite solar technology
. Ricoh is also part of a
consortium with Daiwa House and NTT Anode Energy
that aims to deploy lightweight perovskite modules on buildings.

title: 《江西省增量新能源项目机制电价竞价实施细则（修订版）》政策解读-索比光伏网
content:
近期，江西省发展改革委印发《江西省增量新能源项目机制电价竞价实施细则(修订版)》，自2026年9月19日起执行，原2025年版细则同时废止。新细则在总结首次竞价经验基础上，进一步优化规则设计，推动新能源加速融入电力市场。
此次修订呈现三大变化：
一、容量认定更实事求是
新增因设备选型因素，允许实际并网规模与核准(备案)容量存在一定偏差，给与企业一定容错空间。同步压实企业责任，要求分布式项目全容量并网时必须满足“四可”条件，未投产项目需提交“全容量并网承诺书”。
二、竞价机制更科学合理
将边际机组入选判定门槛由申报电量的30%提高至60%，有效增强项目收益的可预期性。同价项目剩余电量分配由按“装机容量占比”改为按“申报电量占比”，进一步体现企业自主意愿。同时明确在缺乏有效竞争时可合并风电、光伏项目统一竞价。
三、考核管理更精准务实
全面取消未投产项目履约保函要求，减轻企业负担。同时，压缩延期投产超6个月的处罚年限，调整为“取消下一年度投资方(上溯至省级)竞价资格”，惩戒力度与违规程度更加匹配，并新增申报价格“截止后自动封存”规定，防范串通报价风险。
新细则的出台，标志着我省新能源上网电价市场化改革进入常态化、精细化运行新阶段，将为促进新能源高质量发展提供坚实制度保障。

title: The UK and Taiwan launch new CCUS partnership
content:
The UK and Taiwan have launched a new carbon capture, utilisation and storage
(CCUS) partnership during the eighth UK Taiwan Energy Dialogue in Taipei.
The new initiative forms part of the Energy and Net Zero pillar of the
Enhanced Trade Partnership and is designed to strengthen cooperation on
industrial decarbonisation.
The partnership has set out to focus on policy, regulatory and technical
collaboration in addition to commercial pipelines for the CCUS deployment
and future opportunities. These identified workstreams will support efficient
project developments.
It aims to bring together governments, regulators, industry, investors
and research institutions to support the development of CCUS projects in
both markets, ensuring strong cooperation.
Offshore wind was a key topic of discussion. UK officials highlighted the
country's 16.7 GW of installed offshore wind capacity and its target of
reaching 43-50 GW by 2030. Taiwan stated it currently has an estimated
5 GW of installed offshore wind capacity.
Taiwan outlined plans for further offshore wind allocation rounds, stronger
local supply chains, improved financing and preparations for floating wind
demonstration projects.

title: First BC Wind monopiles arrive at Świnoujście
content:
The first monopiles for the 390 MW BC Wind offshore wind farm have officially
arrived at the port of Świnoujście, marking the start of logistical operations
ahead of the project's installation phase.
Once completed, the offshore wind farm will consist of 26 bottom fixed
wind turbines, each with a capacity of 14 MW, generating enough renewable
energy to power approximately 488,000 Polish homes and businesses.
According to the announcement, the milestone reinforces the potential of
Poland's port infrastructure, marking the first time foundations of this
scale have been accepted at a Polish installation port.
Pete Geddes, BC Wind project director, said: "The acceptance of the
first monopiles at a Polish port is an important milestone in the BC Wind
project and another step in the development of the domestic offshore wind
energy sector."
"We are pleased to be able to involve Polish companies in these activities,
creating an opportunity to gain practical experience and develop the skills
of local teams, while supporting the development of the domestic supply
Local companies will support the next stage of operations, including Dynap,
which will be responsible for a range of monopile and transition piece
related tasks. Team Project from Modrzewie will assist in the terminal's
adaptation, ensuring the ground is prepared for unloading foundation structures,
along with carrying out additional works as required.

title: RWE’s SeaMe project completes initial offshore testing
content:
RWE has announced that the SeaMe project (Sustainable Ecosystem Approach
in Monitoring the marine Environment) has officially completed its initial
offshore testing phase after two years.
The project tested a range of innovative technologies in real world conditions,
including drones, AI-assisted camera systems and autonomous underwater
vehicles.
Testing was carried out at RWE’s Kaskasi
offshore wind farm.
The aim of the project is to support environmental monitoring, construction
and operation of offshore wind farms, helping to make the process more
efficient and sustainable.
Tobias Keitel, CEO of RWE Offshore Wind, said: “As one of the world’s
leading companies in offshore wind, we aim to build and operate wind farms
in harmony with nature.”
Adding: “SeaMe demonstrates that innovative technologies can help us gain
an even better understanding of the interactions between offshore wind
energy and marine ecosystems.”
According to the announcement, the project will collect both biological
and physical environmental data. Combined with more frequent observations
and in-depth assessments of the marine environment, this information will
help track the development of marine ecosystems.
RWE said the data will be collected using minimally invasive, low-emission
methods, ensuring that monitoring activities remain both efficient and
environmentally friendly.
