title: New framework aims to support nature-positive offshore wind development
content:
New framework aims to support nature-positive offshore wind development TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
New framework aims to support nature-positive offshore wind development
The Offshore Wind Nature-Positive Contributions Framework has officially
launched under the Global Initiative for Nature, Grids and Renewables (GINGR).
Developed by three organisations, IUCN, the Renewables Grid Initiative
(RGI) and Bluedot Associates Ltd, the framework launches at a time when
offshore wind is becoming an increasingly important part of the renewable
energy transition.
“This framework unites developers, policymakers, financiers and conservation
organisations around a shared approach to credible, measurable biodiversity
contributions from offshore wind,” said Rachel Asante-Owusu, IUCN senior
programme coordinator for energy transition.
According to the announcement, the framework will support offshore wind
projects by providing guidance and tools to help define, measure and deliver
nature-positive contributions.
“The primary reason for developing this framework is to establish how
offshore wind projects can credibly deliver measurable contributions at
the site level while addressing key challenges,” said Neil Cousins, founder
and director of Bluedot Associates.

title: ‘Nobody’s Ready’: AI-Found Bugs Spark a Corporate Security Spending Spree
content: A week ago, Vijay Rayapati, CEO of enterprise software startup Atomicwork, gathered his team of roughly 30 software engineers and told them to drop everything and prioritize cybersecurity. A series of cybersecurity incidents over the prior 48 hours demanded the company’s immediate attention: eMudhra, a so-called root certificate authority, which websites and software makers rely on to prove their identity to users, had been hacked; LiteLLM, a popular open-source tool for routing requests to different AI models, was compromised; and a security vulnerability had been found in PHP, a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. While the startup ultimately verified that it wasn’t directly impacted by the threats, the fact that it was scrambling last week “shows nobody’s ready,” Rayapati said. He is planning to hire one cybersecurity engineer for every three technical hires his company makes, and projects the number of cybersecurity-focused engineers will roughly triple to 27 in the year ahead. Atomicwork is hardly alone. Half a dozen cybersecurity executives in different industries say they’re planning to increase their spending on cybersecurity in the year ahead, including on headcount and software, such as AI agents that aim to be on guard around the clock. The explosion of new vulnerability scanning tools powered by large language models poses a competitive threat to more established products that have been around since before LLMs The scramble stems largely from AI models that are finding software flaws far faster than companies can fix them. Bigger, regulated enterprises have even more to worry about. Bank of America, for instance, recently disclosed it’s hiring 1,000 contractors to work on patching gaps in its software using AI such as Anthropic’s Mythos. Atomicwork CEO Vijay Rayapati, credit: Helen Shanthi, Atomicwork. Other big financial institutions are boosting spending too. Goldman Sachs has been using models like Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra heavily to hunt for bugs in its own software, and Goldman executives have discussed how the firm could soon be on track to spend as much or more on AI for security than it spends on AI coding tools, which has been its biggest AI-related expense, according to someone who spoke to Goldman leadership about it. The firm spends in the millions annually on AI, though its total spending couldn’t be learned. A Goldman spokesperson declined to comment. In another example, a major U.S. energy provider is expanding its roughly $30 million cybersecurity budget by more than 10% this year compared to last year, according to its chief information security officer, who wasn’t authorized to speak publicly about their firm’s strategy. The additional spending is going towards AI like Mythos as well as AI-powered add-ons in security tools it was already using from vendors like Proofpoint, which it used for email protection, and Cisco’s Splunk, which it used to monitor data, this person said. The two security vendors charge extra to use AI that continuously monitors the tools, which this executive said was necessary to prepare for more persistent, AI-powered attacks by hackers, which are fast becoming the norm . The energy firm pulled next year’s cybersecurity budget forward to pay for the additional features, its CISO said. Global IT services firm Diversified experienced a chaotic sprint to respond to the PHP flaw and a new vulnerability reported in Brotli, a widely used open-source library for compressing web traffic, according to Viral Trapathi, its chief information officer. The company directed most of its roughly 100 IT staff, including analysts and engineers who typically don’t work directly on cybersecurity, to investigate which of its cloud applications and webpages could be vulnerable, and to install patches. “These are massive efforts to do the remediation, so it’s a much wider impact than just a straightforward patch. This is taking time away from actual day to day operations,” Tripathi said. Diversified is planning to hire at least three new full-time cybersecurity staff, Tripathi said, and is budgeting roughly 20% more on cybersecurity software in the coming year, including on AI that automates app monitoring. Cybersecurity vendors, whose revenues have already accelerated this year as AI became more useful for cybersecurity, are licking their chops. “This is part of the new norm. Don’t think of this as an emergency one-off, think of this as something you’ll have to do basically every day going forward,” said Lee Klarich, chief product and technology officer at Palo Alto Networks, the biggest standalone provider of cybersecurity. The company’s growth rate doubled in the past two reported quarters, to more than 30%, compared to prior quarters. The increased spending on security software has implications for many companies. OpenAI and Anthropic are each betting on cybersecurity demand to drive their sales in the coming year, thanks in part to companies such as Palo Alto Networks, which use them in their products. And cybersecurity startups that also utilize such models to automate various cybersecurity roles are fielding takeover interest, The Information has reported . “It’s clear that the next three to five years are going to be the most important in the history of the security industry,” said Alex Stamos, who previously led Facebook’s cybersecurity and last month joined AI startup Cognition in the same role. “Defenders had a headstart at getting ready for AI-related risks, in part because we [corporate defenders] have more money. But attackers are already catching up.” An Explosion in Vulnerabilities Even if hackers weren’t using AI in droves right now, the sheer number of vulnerabilities that good-guy security researchers have found this year using AI has put a strain on cybersecurity staff tasked with patching newly discovered gaps. Palo Alto Networks’ Klarich illustrated the scope of the problem. When Anthropic first gave a dozen tech and cybersecurity companies access to its Mythos model in May, the total number of vulnerabilities in open source software that had been reported across the globe that month was roughly 1,500. One month later, the number of new open source vulnerabilities discovered by just those 12 companies using Mythos exceeded 37,000, he said, though not all of the vulnerabilities are severe and not all have been confirmed or publicly reported. And in August and September alone, the number of so-called high-severity vulnerabilities—those that could pose serious threats to sensitive data—that were reported exceeded the total number found in the entirety of 2025, according to research firm Epoch AI. Cybersecurity executives say their spending on AI like Mythos ballooned earlier this year and they’re seeking cost-effective alternatives. UiPath Chief Information Security Officer Scott Roberts, for instance, said the enterprise software firm has recently cut such spending by using cheaper open source models.

title: Foundry Raises $100 Million for Autonomous Factories
content: Large companies have learned over the past couple years that they can get more mileage out of AI agents by rethinking their processes from scratch, rather than merely automating the existing ways of doing things. Manufacturers are beginning to learn the same lesson as they adopt robots powered by physical AI models. One such manufacturer is Foundry , a startup that was founded less than a year ago, which has raised a new round totaling $100 million to build automated factories, the company told The Information exclusively. Marlinspike Partners led the Series A funding round, and Khosla Ventures , which led Foundry’s seed round, participated. Foundry is designing its factories around AI-powered robots, rather than slotting robots into existing production lines. Those robots are organized into work cells that focus on skills such as cabling, fastening and precise placement, rather than making a particular product. Due to that flexibility, Foundry can produce a variety of products for its customers within a single factory, following a manufacturing-as-a-service business model. It currently has a handful of customers in industries including military, energy, autonomous vehicles and telecommunications. “The value of autonomous facilities is that you can build many things under one roof,” said co-founder and CEO Adarsh Kulkarni . “The same model that has really learned fastening can work on satellites and drones and robot dogs and autonomous submarines,” he said. “We build drones on Monday, batteries on Tuesday, satellites on Thursday.” That flexibility comes at the cost of some inefficiency, Kulkarni acknowledged, but he said versatility that enables fast iteration is more valuable to customers. “One mass producing automatic facility is highly efficient, but it's highly efficient in only one axis, which is building a million of exactly the same thing,” he said. “You have basically no design flexibility.” Specialized factories will still make more sense for some mass manufacturing, such as producing iPhones or cars, at least for the next several years, Khosla Ventures founder Vinod Khosla said in an interview. But Foundry’s approach allows it to change the products it makes “rapidly based on market demand in very short cycles,” which opens an opportunity for factories in the U.S. to compete against cheaper labor in China, he argued. “American factories have to be done differently: much more capex efficient, much more product flexible, much more demand responsive, and closer to the demand. You can't have 60-day shipping times,” he said. Kulkarni previously ran the robotics division at Scale AI , the data-labeling startup part-owned by Meta , where he led work on third-party robotics data. His co-founder, Emmanuel Lamacchia , previously ran the Model Y program at Tesla . Foundry recently moved to its first factory in Emeryville, Calif. The facility is about 130,000 square feet. Foundry is still setting it up, but it is already shipping products to paying customers. The factory will eventually hold thousands of robots: primarily industrial arms wielding tools that Foundry develops, in addition to a fleet of vehicles to shuttle partially assembled products from one work cell to another. One type of robot is conspicuously absent at the facility: humanoid robots that walk on two legs. The potential for such machines to automate manufacturing tasks has lifted the valuations of humanoid companies to astronomical heights in recent years, but Foundry’s aversion to humanoids indicates that the market for humanoids could be smaller than some proponents have suggested. “I‘ve done my time with legged robotics, and I love it, and it’s amazing, but humanoids are very inefficient in a lot of ways,” said Kulkarni. “Deploying a humanoid in an existing manual facility might make sense, but if you’re building the building from the ground up, there is no reason you need to depend on that.” (Khosla, who expects highly capable humanoids in the next two years, said he foresees humanoids becoming a “key component” of Foundry’s operations in the future.) Foundry’s robots have their own limitations. Even after being trained for specific manufacturing jobs, AI-powered robots still struggle with some tasks, such as those requiring “micron-level precision,” Kulkarni said. For those tasks, Foundry employs hundreds of human technicians. Data collected from their work will feed into and improve its AI models. The ability to hold onto data from making a wide variety of products is one advantage that Foundry has over companies that sell robots to factories and warehouses, some of which are reluctant to allow an outside company to collect data from their facilities. “It‘s pretty easy for us to negotiate that we own the data,” Kulkarni said. “All of this training data is a byproduct of making our customers’ manufacturing lives easier.” Khosla said that the ability for Foundry’s robots to learn more over time is key. “These are learning factories, so if they learn on assembling defense gizmos, they will apply it to assembling alarm clocks too.” Here’s what else is going on… Big Number Meta Platforms is slightly increasing the size of its planned stock sales to fund AI investments to a total of $97.5 billion from $95 billion, the company said. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Physical Intelligence , which builds AI software for robots, is in talks to raise at least $1 billion at a valuation of roughly $20 billion led by existing backers Avenir and Lux Capital, Bloomberg reported. Approaching.AI , which provides software and hardware for running AI models, raised more than RMB 1.3 billion (roughly $183 million) in a Series B funding round led by Zhejiang Finance Innovation , Xiaoshan Capital , ICBC Investment , Zhongguancun Science City , Xinglian Capital and Qianjiang Century City. Hex Technologies , which provides software to track and analyze AI agents, raised $100 million in funding at a $1.2 billion valuation led by Peak XV Partners. Infisical , which secures AI agents’ access to company credentials, raised $40 million in a Series B funding round at a $600 million valuation led by Elad Gil. Machenta , which creates robotic AI models that can learn new tasks from one demonstration, raised $40 million in a seed funding round led by Creandum and Union Square Ventures. Hyperbolic , which operates a GPU marketplace, raised $30 million in a Series A1 funding round led by Walden Catalyst. Avante , which makes an AI benefits-management platform, raised $30 million in a Series A funding round led by Frist Cressey Ventures. 22one , which builds AI tools for law enforcement, has hit a valuation of nearly $400 million after raising funds from Sequoia , General Catalyst and Lux Capital. Vera Health , which runs an AI clinical-evidence search engine, raised $28.5 million in a Series A funding round led by Threshold Ventures. ClarityCare , which builds AI agents for healthcare payers, raised $16.3 million in a Series A funding round led by Headline. Live2.ai , which helps AI to help brands manage their social media campaigns, raised ₹130 crore (about $14 million) in a pre-Series B funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. Xplore AI , which builds reinforcement learning environments for physical engineering, raised a $11 million seed round co-led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Base10 Partners . The company also released a new benchmark for physical engineering tasks called Real World Engineering Bench . OpenAI plans to buy Google ’s AI chips, The Information reported today, citing a person familiar with the matter. Google and Oracle also announced a partnership that will make Google’s tensor processing units available to Oracle cloud customers, the first time the AI chips would be made available on a hyperscale cloud platform outside of Google’s. As part of OpenAI ’s three science breakthroughs yesterday, its models disproved a foundational theory within cryptography, the AI company claimed on Monday. Anthropic said it acquired Mithril Medicin e, a one-person startup developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy, a sign of the AI developer’s growing ambitions in drug discovery. Xint , an AI cybersecurity firm, said it found a vulnerability that reveals the chains of thought from OpenAI models, rather than just summaries of their reasoning. Justin Sun, founder of the blockchain startup Tron , launched a pilot program for the Justin Sun Prize on Monday. The prize will give awards for up to $1 million for discoveries in mathematics and aims to help integrate AI into math findings while encouraging continued rigor. Axiom , which uses AI to formally verify math and computer code, announced that it had verified a math proof of the “Enormous Theorem” using AI. title: Amazon Hedges Against AI Shopping Agents With 250 Million Outside Listings
content: For more than a year, Amazon has blocked outside shopping agents from its site while finding ways for its own customers to shop elsewhere. Now a new wave of AI assistants like Meta’s Muse is raising the stakes. In recent months Amazon has stepped up its Shop Direct initiative, which promotes products from brands that don’t sell on Amazon’s site, potentially giving shoppers less reason to turn to outside AI tools that can buy across retailers. The company now has 250 million listings that link to products sold elsewhere, about 2.5 times as many as in March, and is highlighting the goods more prominently through curated style edits and other displays on its site. Amazon says it’s continuing to innovate on how and where it’s showing outside products to customers. As part of that, Amazon has added items from big brands such as Alo Yoga and Warby Parker and introduced dedicated pages for showcasing outside listings from brands. It’s also started showing more product details on its own site before shoppers click through to an outside retailer. Amazon has been testing new placements since March. Combined with the surge in Shop Direct listings, the moves represent a significant expansion that mixes in brands’ off-site product listings across Amazon’s selection. Earlier on, the Shop Direct products had mostly appeared in Amazon’s search bar and suggestions in its Alexa shopping chatbot. “Amazon is increasingly a destination where customers can find and buy products not just from our store,” an Amazon spokesperson said. “Tens of millions of customers have discovered hundreds of millions of unique products from other stores through Shop Direct since the program launched, and Shop Direct products are appearing in hundreds of millions of searches monthly. We’re pleased with the foundation we’re building—broad selection, quality search results, and a growing customer response that reinforces our commitment to making every product discoverable, no matter where it’s sold.” Listings on Amazon from non-Amazon websites. Yet for all that growth, the effort remains a mystery to many online merchants. Eleven people who run e-commerce sites or work with merchants, representing hundreds of sellers overall, said they have little insight into when or why outside products show up on Amazon. Those whose products do appear say they’ve seen few sales as a result. Several also said they haven’t heard much from their own Amazon reps in the past six months about Shop Direct. Earlier this month, for instance, e-commerce agency Nectar noticed Amazon listings for products sold on two of its clients’ direct-to-consumer sites, according to Co-CEO Jason Landro. Amazon didn’t tell Nectar or its clients ahead of time that it would be listing the products, and Nectar found out only when the listings went live. Katharine McKee, founder of Morphology Consulting, an e-commerce consultancy that works with around 50 brands across six clients, said Amazon started showing links to buy some clients’ products on other retailers’ sites sometime between late July and October, though she wasn’t sure exactly when they first went live. The listings can come and go on Amazon without notice. Jason Boyce, CEO of e-commerce agency Avenue7Media, said he noticed Amazon showing listings that linked to other retail sites at the end of 2025 that disappeared sometime in the second quarter of this year. Some merchants also say they’ve noticed issues with listings on Amazon that show product information that doesn’t match what they’re actually selling on their sites—the same kind of errors Amazon cited when it blocked outside AI shopping bots last year. CEO Andy Jassy has said outside technology doesn’t offer a good customer experience, though Amazon is open to letting outside shopping tools in if they improve and offer attractive economics. The product links also don’t always go to the brands’ own direct-to-consumer sites. For one wellness brand, Amazon directed shoppers to a page from a retailer that isn’t an authorized reseller of the products, McKee said. Scaling up Shop Direct could represent a big change for Amazon, which has long moved cautiously with major changes to its retail site, the heart of its $588 billion commerce and ads business. The company launched outside product listings in Amazon in February 2025 and two months later added a Buy for Me feature, which uses agents to complete outside purchases without leaving Amazon’s site, moves that came as OpenAI and Google were gearing up to add AI checkouts. AI shopping has had false starts before, with OpenAI scrapping a high-profile ChatGPT checkout push in March, and using AI to buy things is far from a mainstream consumer habit. Still, signs are emerging that the latest crop of AI consumer apps is starting to actually generate orders—and could represent an eventual threat to Amazon’s dominant role in how people shop online. Omar Qari, CEO of e-commerce software seller Logicbroker, said his clients have seen a handful of Muse orders in the past few weeks while not seeing many Shop Direct–driven sales since the Amazon program began. “I was just surprised that anybody” was shopping via an agent, Qari said. Amazon’s Reach Amazon has pushed beyond its own site before with services like Buy with Prime, which lets outside merchants offer Amazon’s checkout and speedy delivery, features they actively select. With Shop Direct, merchants have to opt out of inclusion. Amazon says the technology powering its AI shopping features crawls publicly available data, much as other tools do, and abides by websites’ robots.txt instructions on what bots are allowed. Merchants are considered for Shop Direct unless they ask to be excluded, an option Amazon says has been in place since the program first launched. The features sparked blowback early this year from some merchants who complained that they were included without a heads-up, and who said the feature pulled incorrect product details that led to erroneous orders. Still, some who work with online brands, including ones that sell on sites powered by e-commerce giant Shopify, saw potential benefits in features that provided visibility on Amazon. “If you’re going to put our Shopify listings on Amazon in front of a billion people, great, more money for us. [Amazon has] much better reach than our Shopify site,” said McKee, the e-commerce consultant. At the same time, Amazon has had to grapple with the same challenges other agentic shopping efforts face. Retail sites, rife with features like pop-up windows and promo codes for new shoppers, are hard for AI tools to navigate , and pricing and in-stock information can quickly go stale. Early on, Amazon’s shopping agent software, built around Anthropic models, had trouble navigating some retail websites, according to people with knowledge of the project. Amazon also had to direct the agent to check sites frequently to get current product data, and engineers needed to confirm the AI’s findings, one person with knowledge of the project said. In March, Amazon announced more integrations with a number of e-commerce feed providers, which compile retailers’ product information in real time. Those included Feedonomics, owned by Shopify competitor Commerce (formerly BigCommerce), as well as Salsify and CedCommerce. Amazon recently added another provider, VersaFeed. Amazon says it’s choosing which products to show through Shop Direct based on the quality of the product listing and whether something is in stock, among other factors. It has received requests from large and small brands alike asking to be included. Amazon is also laying the groundwork for brands to better track the sales Shop Direct drives. The company says that, based on URL tags added to links to show where visitors come from, companies can see what traffic Shop Direct is driving to their sites. Amazon is also building more reporting capabilities to track the benefits of showing up in Shop Direct.

title: Bumble Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd Explains Decision to Take Company Private
content: Bumble cofounder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd said on Tuesday a sale of her 12-year-old dating app was important for the “for the longevity of Bumble’s mission” given the way the public markets had treated the company, whose stock had dropped to near $2. Herd said she would “disassociate” watching the stock price but was newly optimistic about Bumble’s future after new tech investment firm Ithaca Holdings agreed to take the company private in a $1.3 billion deal announced earlier this month. “I felt like I was stuck under a wave for like five years,” she said at The Information’s WTF Summit , in her first interview since Bumble agreed to a sale. “But now I’m on the beach.” Herd said she expected the company to take advantage of AI to modernize a product she said had become disconnected from the “revolutionary technology at the tips of your fingers today,” such as Anthropic’s Claude. She said Bumble could use AI to introduce more people to relevant events and groups of people, feeding what she termed as an “absolute craving of meeting people out in the world again.” As part of the deal, Wolfe Herd will step down as CEO, ceding the role to Ithaca Holdings founders Ravi Gupta, a former Sequoia Capital general partner, and former Meta Platforms executive John Hegeman, who will serve as co-CEOs. Wolfe Herd, who founded the company in 2014 with the unique feature that women would send the first message to a potential date, said she will remain involved and an “active shareholder.” She said she plans to continue being involved in the brand. “I’m not a technologist,” she said. “This is not my area of expertise. Like, you want me to build you a brand? Call me. I got you.” Wolfe Herd abstained from voting on the deal, which was unanimously approved by the rest of Bumble’s board. Still, she was optimistic about the sale, which she described as “the best outcome for the way the public markets were viewing our business.” Bumble went public in 2021 at a roughly $14 billion valuation. Its market cap has since sunk to less than $1 billion amid a decline in revenue and a drop in paying users. As for why the company has struggled in recent years, Wolfe Herd blamed fatigue among users in their 20s and 30s, who she said have just gotten “really, really overexposed to technology.” But she maintained there is still demand for dating apps, even as the broader industry has struggled. “Fundamentally speaking, the demand for love and connection I would argue is stronger today than when I started the company,” she said. The company has been making changes to its core features. Earlier this year, the company announced it was rethinking its core swipe feature (Wolfe Herd said “swipe is still breathing” though suggested it is being rethought) and introducing a new AI assistant called Bee that would help with the matchmaking process. According to Wolfe Herd, the company will also focus on using AI to improve the quality of suggested matches and for improving safety on the platform. “This can be a company that outlives me and that’s why I’ve hung on so long. And I don’t say that in some weird, delusional founder narrative,” she explained. “I just really do believe in this.”

title: Chipmaker Onsemi in Talks to Buy Startup for About $1 Billion
content: Semiconductor component maker Onsemi has been discussing an acquisition of 16-year-old chip startup Ferric for close to $1 billion, say people familiar with the matter—a deal that reflects growing demand for technology that can manage the intense energy needs of AI chips. Onsemi’s talks with Ferric follow a similar acquisition by rival Analog Devices, which in May agreed to pay $1.5 billion to buy Empower Semiconductor, a 12-year-old startup whose devices help AI chips manage electricity more efficiently. It isn’t clear how the Onsemi deal is being structured. It could include payments to Ferric based on performance targets. An Onsemi deal for Ferric could come together in the coming days, though discussions are ongoing and deal terms could change or fall apart, the people said. Onsemi is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on Monday. A spokesperson for Onsemi didn’t respond to requests for comments. A spokesperson for Ferric declined to comment. Onsemi, which has a market cap of about $30 billion, designs and makes semiconductors that manage the power needs of cars, factories and, increasingly, AI data centers. As the demand for electricity from these data centers grows, chipmakers are on the hunt for new technologies that can deliver energy to a chip with less waste. Traditionally, chip designers such as Onsemi and Analog Devices have handled power consumption by placing power management chips next to the processor on a circuit board and running electricity horizontally across the circuit board. These chips act as a central system to monitor and distribute electrical power. Startups like Ferric make so-called integrated voltage regulators and their devices can funnel power directly to thin, small chips underneath or inside the AI chips. The design cuts the distance the electricity needs to travel, reducing the energy lost along the way. Scottsdale, Ariz.-based Onsemi, which generated $6 billion in revenue last year, has been trying to expand its business lines.  This month, it agreed to buy publicly-traded Synaptics for $5.7 billion in cash, a deal that could help it to expand its sales of sensors and processors in smart devices. Founded in 2010, New York-based Ferric raised venture funding from New Science Ventures and received grants from the federal government, according to PitchBook. A price tag of close to $1 billion would be a steep price for a startup generating little revenue.

title: Google is Having a TPU Moment
content: Get ready to hear Google brag about TPUs on Wednesday. When Alphabet, Google’s parent company, reports third-quarter earnings tomorrow, the company’s in-house AI chips, tensor processing units, are sure to be on the lips of Google executives and Wall Street analysts. That’s because we got a bunch of new  signs this week of the swelling customer demand for TPUs. Earlier today, Google said that Oracle will become the first major cloud provider outside Google itself to begin offering TPUs to customers through its own data centers. And a short while ago, Ryan Barwick published a scoop for us that says OpenAI—a major customer for Nvidia’s AI chips—plans to buy Google’s TPUs. But perhaps the juiciest details on TPU demand came on Monday courtesy of Anthropic’s IPO prospectus. In that filing, Anthropic chronicled the enormity of the financial commitment it has made to the Google chips, including a plan to spend $114.5 billion with Google Cloud (it didn’t specify how much of that will be for TPU-based compute). Anthropic also estimated it could spend an additional $125 billion to $150 billion on TPUs with Google and other providers. And the AI company will pony up $161.2 billion for TPU compute with Broadcom, which co-designs TPUs with Google. TPUs, you’ll recall, began as chips that Google used only internally starting over a decade ago. The company began allowing outside customers to use them via Google Cloud in 2018. More recently, Google has begun striking agreements with companies like Fluidstack and now Oracle to run TPUs in their own data centers. Google only began recognizing revenue from the sale of TPUs to outside data centers last quarter, though Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi said on an earnings call then that only a small portion of the revenues from its TPU agreements were reflected during that period. The “vast majority of revenues” from those agreements will kick in next year, Ashkenazi said. Analysts are predicting something of a windfall for Google when that happens. In a report earlier this month, TD Cowen’s John Blackledge estimated that TPUs will generate $9.4 billion in sales during the second half of this year, about 13% of the roughly $70 billion in revenue he was forecasting for Google Cloud during that period. By 2028, Blackledge thinks TPUs could be a $138 billion business, accounting for 34% of Google Cloud’s estimated revenue that year. While big, that figure would still be a fraction of the $692 billion in revenue that analysts, on average, are expecting Nvidia, the dominant provider of AI chips, to report in its fiscal year ending January 2028. Still, Google’s TPU growth has not gone unnoticed at Nvidia. Today, we got further evidence of Nvidia’s efforts to keep marquee companies in its tent. The chipmaker announced an expansion of its partnership with Meta, which said it would increase its deployment of Nvidia chips. As part of the agreement, Nvidia will invest $3 billion into the nearly $100 billion in stock offerings that Meta announced this week. We reported earlier this year that Meta struck a deal to rent TPUs from Google. Nvidia isn’t going to let Google invade its turf without a fight. In Other News Meta increased the size of its planned stock sales to $97.5 billion from $95 billion. The offerings will help the company raise money for its AI investments. Anthropic said it has begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb, BigHat Biosciences and other pharmaceutical companies to use AI in drug discovery. Anthropic also said it acquired a small company, Mithril Medicine, working on treatments for rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Anduril and Qualcomm said they’re working together to build rugged laptops in the U.S. aimed at government, defense, first responders and other customers. The companies are calling the line of computers BlueChip. title: OpenAI, a Longtime Nvidia Customer, Plans to Buy Google’s AI Chips
content: OpenAI plans to buy Google ’s AI chips, according to a person familiar with the matter, in a boost for a rising competitor to OpenAI backer Nvidia. Financial terms and other details of OpenAI’s planned purchase couldn’t be learned. But any deal for it to buy tensor processing units would be a big win for Google’s chip business, which is a growing challenger to the Nvidia graphics processing units that have dominated the market for AI computing power. OpenAI has been one of the most valuable customers for Nvidia, which in turn has invested tens of billions of dollars in the startup. In August, Nvidia also agreed to provide more than $100 billion in credit support for a massive Ohio-based data center project planned for OpenAI and built exclusively using Nvidia’s chip stack. At the time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote in a blog that OpenAI had committed to spending roughly $600 billion to use Nvidia servers through 2030. OpenAI’s plans for Google chips come as it seeks to hire an engineer to “lead the optimization” of OpenAI’s state-of-the-art frontier models on TPUs. Google, meanwhile, scored a separate win for its chip business with its announcement Tuesday that Oracle will become the first major cloud provider outside Google to rent out TPUs to customers. A person familiar with that agreement said that Oracle is purchasing the chips and that large mutual customers of the two companies will be the TPUs’ users. The customers’ identities couldn’t be learned. OpenAI is a major cloud customer of Oracle and last week announced plans to make its models available through Google Cloud. OpenAI also has been renting Nvidia chips from Google Cloud. Google developed its TPUs more than a decade ago and says they are more efficient than Nvidia’s GPUs. Google has rented TPUs out of its own cloud facilities for years to customers including Anthropic (which trained its models on the chips) and Apple as well as trading firms such as Citadel Securities and startups. Google more recently began selling its TPUs to other data center operators and users starting with neoclouds such as Fluidstack. Last year, The Information reported that OpenAI had begun using Google’s TPUs, lessening the company’s reliance on Nvidia’s chips. That prompted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to spring to action, and Nvidia and OpenAI then worked on a new deal. An OpenAI spokesperson later said the company did not have “current plans to use TPUs specifically.” The OpenAI job listing indicated that OpenAI’s efforts to optimize its models for TPUs are at an early stage, saying the position will have “broad technical ownership” of the effort. “We welcome experience gained through either training or inference, with a strong foundation in optimizing real workloads on TPUs,” the listing said.

title: Is Anduril Worth $120 Billion?
content: Some senior employees at Anduril Industries have indicated to investors that the autonomous weapons maker hopes to raise a new funding round in the first quarter next year, I’ve learned. It has considered doing so at a valuation of around $120 billion, according to people with knowledge of the conversations. Given that the prospective round is months away, though, it’s too soon to know it will happen for sure at this price. “No decisions have been made about any future financing, and anyone claiming knowledge of its terms, structure, pricing or timing is speculating or misinformed,” an Anduril spokesperson told me. “As a private company, we regularly evaluate opportunities to fund the growth of the business.” If Anduril does raise at a $120 billion valuation, it would be a steep increase to an ongoing employee share sale at a $90 billion valuation and about double the valuation of its most recent funding round, a $5 billion financing announced in May at $61 billion . It’s also higher than the $100 billion valuation Reuters reported the munitions maker was discussing in July. Recent contract wins could justify such a sizable valuation jump: In September, the U.S. Army awarded Anduril a nearly $163 million contract to expand the use of its software platform, Lattice, within the Army. That contract could become as large as $1.8 billion over the next five years. More contracts like these would help boost Anduril’s revenue, which is still small compared to that of large defense contractors: The company earlier this year forecast that its revenue will rise to $4.3 billion this year, more than double last year—just a sliver of the more than $80 billion Lockheed Martin, which has a market cap of about $144 billion, expects to generate this year. Now on to Anthropic… When Spark Capital first invested in Anthropic in early 2023, the model maker had only raised money from wealthy investors like Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX co-founder, and Jaan Tallinn, Skype co-founder. The older OpenAI had more cash and talent, and Anthropic was barely generating any revenue, we reported at the time . But Spark General Partner Yasmin Razavi—alongside Factorial Funds, started by Sol Bier, a former Cruise Automation engineer, and Sound Ventures—figured there was room for another large language model maker. Spark invested about $75 million, its biggest single investment at the time, leading Anthropic’s Series C that year. If Anthropic’s initial public offering values it at $1.5 trillion, those shares would have been worth 80 times what Spark paid. But Anthropic’s IPO filing, made public on Monday , showed just how aggressively the 21-year-old venture fund has added to its investment since the first check. Spark came into every funding round after the C, snapping up a total of 12.2 million shares for just under $777 million, according to the securities filing. Over 56% of that money is from Spark’s investment in Anthropic’s $65 billion Series H in May, raised on the heels of Claude Code’s breakout success. That round valued the model maker at $965 billion including the investment, and Spark sunk nearly $440 million into it (That huge check didn’t even earn Spark a mention in Anthropic’s press release , where it focused on co-leads like Sequoia Capital, which invested more than $2 billion into the round.) If Anthropic debuts at a valuation of $1.5 trillion, Spark’s slice of Anthropic could be worth over $11 billion, according to our estimates. At a cost basis of under a billion, plus a little IPO dilution, Spark could haul in $9 billion or more—a windfall its limited partners, such as the Orange County Employees Retirement System, will certainly be pleased with. (Spark was already making plans to raise a $3 billion fund, in part off the Anthropic momentum, we reported in March.) Most of the investments seem to come out of Spark’s fourth, fifth and sixth growth funds, according to the footnotes in Anthropic’s S-1. It’s also possible that Spark, like many venture capital firms that have coughed up hundreds of millions of dollars to invest in one round, may have tapped other capital vehicles, such as limited partner co-investment pools, which I wrote about last week . These vehicles are similar in structure to a traditional fund but make fewer, and bigger, investments—often at a discounted fee to their limited partners. In 2023, investing in a foundation model company was somewhat new for Spark. The generalist firm had cut its teeth with breakout consumer tech bets such as Postmates, Discord and Twitter as well as fintech startups like Plaid and Deel. Razavi, who led the firm’s investment in Deel in 2020, is enthusiastic about the wide-ranging use cases for Anthropic’s tech. “The speed of adoption and breadth of applications—across law, medicine, accounting, software development, mining, agriculture, and beyond—are unlike anything we’ve seen before,” Razavi wrote in a Medium post that announced the firm’s Anthropic investment in 2023. “At the heart of all of this lies helpful, harmless, and honest technologies like Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude.” Razavi’s conviction in the company also clinched her a coveted board seat. She is still the only venture capitalist on Anthropic’s board. title: Why Cheaper Models Won't Win OpenAI the Enterprise
content: OpenAI is trying to chip away at Anthropic’s lead with enterprises by fashioning itself as a cheaper, more flexible provider, Steph and I reported this weekend . But Anthropic's impressive prospectus for an initial public offering , filed Monday, shows OpenAI will need to do a lot more than that to really move the needle. To be sure, OpenAI has done a great job getting companies like Rippling to switch to its cost-efficient models from Anthropic’s. In fact, compared to Google and Anthropic, OpenAI has released the least expensive models this year when it comes to completing tasks in evaluations run by research firm Artificial Analysis. For instance, the most cost-efficient model OpenAI released in 2026, GPT-6 Luna with a low reasoning setting, was 45% less expensive than Google’s cheapest model, Gemma E4B, and 80% less than Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5. But as we noted in our piece this weekend, the aftermath of Anthropic’s release of a not-cheap but very capable model, Opus 5.5, in late September took some of the wind out of OpenAI’s sails, at least among customers of OpenRouter, a service businesses use to access different models from one place. That’s a not-so-surprising signal that model capabilities still remain a dominant factor in customers’ eyes. And it adds more urgency to the all-hands-on-deck effort at OpenAI to launch its next major model safely . While Anthropic’s prospectus only covered the first half of the year and didn’t include the third quarter, it showed off strong business metrics. (We already know its growth rate slowed considerably between the second and third quarters , though it was still excellent. And Anthropic is almost certainly at least 40% bigger than OpenAI in terms of revenue.) For instance, Anthropic said that as of Sept. 30, its net revenue retention was 900%, meaning it’s generating nine times more revenue from existing customers, on average, compared to the same period a year ago. (That figure excludes fixed-price Claude Pro and Max subscriptions, which Anthropic says don’t capture changes in spending the way usage-based products, which account for the vast majority of its revenue, do). In addition, the number of enterprises that spent $100,000 or more on Anthropic products in the past 12 months rose more than 12 times to around 11,900. Anthropic is looking to lock in its lead by getting customers to sign longer contracts. The company said in its filing that more enterprise customers are signing non-cancelable, annual or multiyear contracts with minimum spend commitments. Right now, Anthropic doesn’t have such contracts with many of its top customers. Given Anthropic’s commitment to leasing $657 billion in computing capacity over the next seven to 10 years, it may want to lock in some long term contracts with its customers. Fighting the Narrative While OpenAI turns itself into a budget option for enterprises, Anthropic is fighting the narrative that it’s a budget buster . Anthropic lately has taken steps to show its models are also getting cheaper to use. It said last month that Opus 5.5 cost 40% less to complete a task than an earlier version of the model, Opus 5, and it said Monday that the model motivated “many” customers to switch to using that model rather than older Anthropic models. And earlier this month, Anthropic said its newest Haiku model was 75% cheaper to run, compared to an earlier version of the same model. Also in its prospectus, Anthropic said its most capable model, Fable 5.1, was 25% cheaper to use than its earlier flagship, Fable 5. For all the hype around the technology, Anthropic showed that the market has barely taken off. In its prospectus, Anthropic said its products account for less than 1% of the expenses of its largest Fortune 500 customers, and therefore their spending has a lot of room to grow. For other Fortune 500 clients that spend at least $100,000, but less than the top customers, Anthropic products account for less than 0.1% of their total expenses. This represents an opportunity for OpenAI and other AI providers too. But first, these companies have to show that AI can take a share of a company's labor budget, not just replace legacy software or applications. While Anthropic itself has said its engineers are five times more productive now than they were just six months ago, due to Claude, the vast majority of companies won’t be able to match Anthropic’s efficiency for some time. Here’s what else is going on… Ex-GitHub CEO Launches Competitor After GitHub experienced several months of prolonged outages earlier this year, many customers bemoaned the fact that there were so few viable alternatives, we reported this spring . Now, former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke—who left the Microsoft-owned developer services firm last summer—has officially launched a competitor to GitHub. Dohmke’s company, Entire , on Monday announced a new coding repository product where customers can upload and collaborate on code, similar to how people work together in a Google Doc. But unlike GitHub, Entire, which has raised $60 million from Felicis and other backers—says it was purpose-built for AI agents, including features that make it easier to track what AI coding agents are doing and explain why they took specific actions. Whether Entire can take a bite out of GitHub’s pie remains to be seen, but Dohmke is betting that his former employer is ripe for disruption. —Aaron Holmes Upcoming Events Monday, November 9 — Intimate Dinner with The Information and EY Consulting in San Francisco Trust is quickly becoming the defining question of the AI era. title: The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
content:
The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data.
He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions.
Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups.
—Matthew King
Are we there yet? Interspecies communication
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us.
Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex.
Find out how close we are to interspecies communication.
—Cassandra Willyard
This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.
A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

title: Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control
content:
In partnership with
Industrial intelligence
Living digital twins are helping industrial plants run more like living systems, and setting the stage for industries that work in sync.
Most people associate industrial environments with cold steel and clockwork machinery. Functionally, though, a plant or factory is more like a living thing: It has a pulse, even a metabolism. It goes through wear and tear as it ages, and signs of deteriorating health often show up as barely perceptible irregularities.
Digital twin technology has long aimed to mirror that dynamism and model anomalies that may be symptomatic of larger problems. But earlier implementations were a few beats behind physical reality; they were incapable of real-time analysis and unable to proactively address any issues detected. They focused more on simulation, observation and what-if scenario planning, rather than closed-loop execution. Rather than serving as a digital mirror of reality that can spot anomalies or suggest optimizations, a living digital twin combines a dynamic, high-fidelity digital representation of complex operations with the capacity to intervene in the physical world through operations and control systems.
AI is at the center of this change. Rob McGreevy, chief product officer at AVEVA, likens newer, AI-infused digital twins to organisms that grow and evolve. These “living” versions are adaptive, evergreen models of a plant’s assets and processes. Because they keep pace with live conditions and connect systems that once ran in isolation, they provide a previously missing layer of visibility and orchestration that better reflects the organic rhythms of the facility itself.
Now, agentic AI is also enabling industrial systems to move beyond diagnostics or suggestions and act of their own accord. As the technology progresses toward greater autonomy, it’s starting to develop the reflexes for a kind of industrial homeostasis, in which small, constant adjustments keep a plant or factory healthy and humming.
All that said, human judgment and operator oversight still play an instrumental role by defining what healthy looks like to begin with—and flagging when AI systems are falling out of alignment. Living digital twins provide the means for human engineers to monitor what AI is doing and ensure execution is on track.
technologies
Living digital twins link engineering and design information with real-time operational data through a digital thread, or a connected record of an asset that follows it through its lifecycle. A couple of notable technological shifts have helped string this thread together: Sensors (which have gotten more affordable in recent years) now stream telemetry from IoT devices and industrial control equipment, and software platforms bring that information into user-friendly interfaces. Predictive and physics-based models can also provide AI-enriched insights into how a machine or process might behave.

The lenses through which operators view digital twins have evolved in turn. “You can look at the digital twin through the lens of sustainability: What are my emissions?” says McGreevy. “Or, through the lens of maintenance: Is this asset performing in a healthy way? Or, through a performance metric: Is it producing the number of widgets I need?”
boundaries
semi-autonomous
The next phase is letting AI act on select insights those lenses illuminate. For their part, manufacturers are eager for this chapter: In a 2026 Manufacturing Leadership Council
survey of manufacturers
(opens in new tab)
, 66% said they are using or plan to use agentic AI in their operations, and 40% expect some degree of factory autonomy by 2030. At the same time, they’re wary of the potential risks: In
Deloitte’s 2025 smart manufacturing survey
(opens in new tab)
, 65% of executives ranked operational risk, including the potential for business disruption, among their top concerns.

“There is a lot more refinement to be done, a lot more proof points, testing, and validation needed,” McGreevy says about the ongoing process of making AI autonomous. In the near term, McGreevy expects agentic AI to follow the path seen in other industrial technologies like SCADA systems. “The ‘S’ in SCADA means supervisory, and supervisory means there’s a human in the middle,” he says. He sees AI working mostly in that advisory mode for the foreseeable future, with full autonomy limited to narrow, highly repetitive tasks.
As for the role human operators play, the day-to-day is evolving. Workers who once specialized in a single process line or maintenance task can now take on multiple disciplines. They can spend less time and effort approving routine actions one by one, and more on defining acceptable operating limits. Because AI can reinforce patterns in the data it receives, catching missteps early is a core part of the job. Human knowledge and experience in interpreting what AI is seeing and doing is instrumental.
Governance on a company- and industry-wide scale, too, needs to adapt to the times. Organizations must establish clear guardrails for which decisions AI can make on its own and how its actions are monitored and audited. Still, many have yet to set up comprehensive safeguards: In a recent study from
AVEVA and IMD
(opens in new tab)
, 43% of organizations said AI has changed decision-making and accountability across ecosystem partners only slightly or not at all, while just 23% reported a significant or fundamental change. (Only 27% reported sharing data substantially or extensively with partners.)
In the meantime, regulators are starting to define some of the rules. The EU AI Act classifies certain AI safety components used in critical infrastructure as high-risk and imposes requirements for human oversight. Companies are setting up their own structures as well; AVEVA, for one, has a responsible AI governance board and a published set of principles for how AI is developed and deployed.
Real-world
Inside the semi-autonomous systems already running, that oversight looks different from one deployment to another. In some cases, an operator approves every action; in others, AI acts on its own while people oversee and define the boundaries it can operate within. McGreevy cites several examples of what machine autonomy and human-plus-machine collaboration looks like among AVEVA customers:
At Saudi Aramco’s Yanbu refinery, optimization algorithms adjust production in a closed loop, with operators overseeing as needed. At its Ras Tanura refinery, the algorithms recommend changes, and operators decide whether to implement them.
Nestlé uses AI optimization at Nesquik plants to tune the industrial dryers used to produce powdered beverage ingredients. In a landmark test, this tuning reduced energy use by 16%, while improving quality and yield.
At Thailand’s SCG Chemicals, an AI-supported digital twin spanning engineering, operations, and maintenance monitors asset health and flags potential failures. The company reports 99% plant reliability and a ninefold return on investment within six months.
The National Laboratory of the Rockies in the U.S. has built a generative AI model for grid control rooms to provide oversight at scale. The model supports operators with renewable energy forecasting and estimates of grid conditions.
The same synchronization that was once missing from individual plants’ technology systems has also been lacking on a larger scale. “Manufacturing and critical infrastructure have operated as siloed systems for the last 50 years,” says McGreevy. But certain emerging technologies, he suggests, are creating opportunities for more holistic coordination.
On an enterprise level, this might involve the integration of physical AI: systems that pair robotics and sensing technologies with AI-powered decision-making. Drones that fly over pipelines and power lines, for instance, can feed visual inspection data to algorithms that spot gas leaks and other hazards. Not only does this create a more accurate and interconnected flow of information, but it spares humans from needing to physically enter potentially dangerous environments. “The robotics-meets-software convergence will mean fewer incidents, fewer outages, and a more sustainable way of operating,” McGreevy predicts.

A bigger-picture version extends beyond any one plant or process to entire industrial networks, something McGreevy dubs the “integrated value chain.” “Living digital twins make digital manifestations of the entire value chain possible,” he says. “This allows companies to react quickly to supply chain changes, demand changes, tariffs, and material availability.”
Amid today’s realities of turbulent geopolitics and shifting regulatory demands, such resilience will be “an absolute necessity,” adds McGreevy. “Without it, it will be very hard to run an effective business.”

Professor Jean Pierre Bergmann und sein Forschungsteam von der Technischen Universität Ilmenau haben den Thüringer Forschungspreis 2026 in der Kategorie „Angewandte Forschung“ gewonnen. Mit den Forschungsarbeiten zum Schweißen mit Hochleistungslasern gelang es dem Team des Fachgebiets Fertigungstechnik, den durch ungewollte Spritzer verursachten Masseverlust eines Werkstücks um über 90 Prozent zu reduzieren, was für verarbeitende Betriebe weniger Ausschuss, niedrigere Kosten für die Nacharbeit und eine nachhaltigere Produktion bedeutet. Der Thüringer Forschungspreis wird seit 1995 vom Freistaat Thüringen in den Kategorien „Grundlagenforschung“ und „Angewandte Forschung“ vergeben.
Die Photonik-Industrie ist in Thüringen ein wirtschaftliches Schwergewicht. Kein anderer Standort in Deutschland bietet eine vergleichbare Dichte an Spezialisten für Optik, Lasertechnik, Produktionstechnik und Präzisionstechnologien. Mit 195 Unternehmen, einen Umsatz von vier Milliarden Euro und fast 20.000 Beschäftigten in Industrie und Forschung zählt die Photonik zu einem der wichtigsten Wirtschaftsbranchen in Thüringen. Doch beim Schweißen mit Hochleistungslasern – etwa in der Automobil- oder Medizintechnik – gab es für die Industrie bislang ein großes Problem: Will man schneller schweißen, um effizienter zu produzieren, steigt die Zahl der Fehler sprunghaft an. Besonders gravierend: Spritzer. Diese winzigen, flüssigen Metallpartikel werden aus dem Schmelzbad geschleudert, zerstören die Oberfläche des Fertigungsteils und machen aufwändige und teure Nacharbeiten nötig.
Dem Forscherteam um Professor Jean Pierre Bergmann, Leiter des Fachgebiets Fertigungstechnik an der TU Ilmenau, gelang es mit einem neuartigen Schweißverfahren, den Masseverlust durch Spritzer um über 90 Prozent zu reduzieren. Für die kleinen und mittleren Betriebe des verarbeitenden Gewerbes, die Thüringen prägen, bedeutet das weniger Ausschuss, niedrigere Kosten und eine nachhaltigere Produktion.
Um Spritzer beim Laserschweißen zu verhindern, musste das Forscherteam der Ilmenauer Fertigungstechnik zunächst verstehen, was während des Schweißvorgangs im Inneren des Werkstücks passiert, dort, wo das Auge nicht hineinschauen kann. Aber modernste Techniken wie Hochgeschwindigkeitskameras, Bildverarbeitung und Simulationen – und der Teilchenbeschleuniger der European Synchrotron Radiation Facility im französische Grenoble, eine europäische Forschungseinrichtung, die wie ein riesiges, extrem starkes Mikroskop funktioniert. Mit hochenergetischer sogenannter Synchrotronstrahlung – dem weltweit intensivsten Röntgenlicht, das milliardenfach heller ist als herkömmliche Röntgengeräte – kann sie Materie durchleuchten und die Struktur von Atomen und Molekülen bis ins kleinste Detail sichtbar machen.
In hochauflösenden Scans bekamen die Ilmenauer Forscher die extrem schnellen Vorgänge im Inneren der Dampfkapillare, der winzigen, mit Metalldampf gefüllten Kanäle, die beim Tiefschweißen entstehen, in Echtzeit zu sehen. Die Aufnahmen zeigten: Spritzer entstehen durch ein komplexes Zusammenspiel von Metalldampf, Schmelzbadwellen und instabilen Kapillaren. Mithilfe von computergestützten Strömungssimulationen gelang es dem Forschungsteam erstmals, ein vollständiges Modell dieser Mechanismen zu entwickeln.
Dieses tiefe Verständnis der Prozesse, die sich beim Laserschweißen im Innern des Werkstücks abspielen, erlaubte es den Forschern, gezielte Gegenmaßnahmen gegen die Spritzerbildung zu entwickeln. Intelligente Strahlprofile, etwa mit überlagerten Strahlenformen, verlangsamen die Schmelzbadströmungen und erleichtern so das Entweichen von Metalldampf, eine der Ursachen für die ungewollten Spritzer. Zudem positionierten sie Gasdüsen so präzise, dass die Wechselwirkung zwischen Gas und Schmelze zu einer Reduzierung der Spritzer führte.
Die Ergebnisse der Forschungsarbeiten und ein daraus abgeleitete Patent „made in Thüringen“ wurden bereits in Fachzeitschriften veröffentlicht, sodass High-Tech-Laser in der Industrie weltweit präziser, effizienter und kostengünstiger arbeiten.

Kultur geht vor – Die Leipziger Museologie und Museumsvermittlung auf der „MUTEC“
Einer der 159 Aussteller der „MUTEC“ ist die Fakultät Informatik und Medien der HTWK Leipzig. In Halle 4 Stand C23 haben Studierende der Studiengänge Museologie und Museumspädagogik | Bildung und Vermittlung im Museum wieder einen eigenen Ausstellungsstand erarbeitet. Gemeinsam mit Prof. Dr. Gisela Weiß, HTWK-Professorin für Museumspädagogik, informieren sie über aktuelle Trends und Herausforderungen in der Museumsbranche.
Die Museumsstudiengänge bereichern zudem das Fachprogramm im MUTEC Forum (Halle 4, C26): Am Donnerstag moderiert Prof. Dr. Alina Gromova, HTWK-Professorin für Museumstheorie und -strategie, um 11 Uhr das Eröffnungspanel „Museen im Wandel – wie Technologien und soziale Herausforderungen kulturelle Institutionen verändern“ und Prof. Weiß um 16:30 Uhr das Panel „Gemeinsam mehr bewegen – Museumsarbeit im Verbund“. Vorgestellt werden die Potenziale des Museumsdokumentationssystems DigiCULT zur Erschließung, Veröffentlichung und Vernetzung von Objektsammlungen sowie das Pilotprojekt „Sammeln/Entsammeln“ des Museumsverbandes Sachsen-Anhalt. Mitgewirkt haben die Museumsstudiengänge außerdem an der Jury des MUTEC Awards: Am Freitag um 13 Uhr werden zwölf zukunftsweisende Ausstellungsprojekte prämiert.
Angewandte Holzbauforschung – Das FLEX.institut auf der „denkmal“
Die „denkmal“ wird erstmals mit einer Panel-Diskussion zum Thema „Wir viel Denkmal können wir uns leisten?“ (Halle 2, F51) am Donnerstag um 10 Uhr eröffnet, die von HTWK-Professor Dr. Alexander Stahr moderiert wird. Er und sein Team vom FLEX.institut sind zugleich mitverantwortlich für eine weitere Transfer-Innovation auf der Messe. Mit dem Bauunternehmen Bennert entwickelten sie das Konzept für das DENK(M)AreaL. Auf fast 1.000 Quadratmetern Ausstellungsfläche (Halle 2, L15) präsentieren sich 18 Unternehmen, Wissenschaftseinrichtungen und Projektinitia-tiven, darunter die Forschenden von FLEX am Gemeinschaftsstand mit Bennert (Halle 2, L19).
Zur DENK(M)AreaL gehört auch eine Bühne mit einem eigenen Vortragsprogramm. Den Rahmen dafür bildet das 3,5 Meter hohe Konstruktionsmodell des geplanten Pfalzturm-Projektes, in dem das FLEX.institut mit dem Laserinstitut Hochschule Mittweida als Projektpartner der Universität Kaiserslautern-Landau agiert. Insgesamt 19 Vorträge über kreative Lösungsansätze zu aktuellen Fragen des Bauens im Bestand sowie der Denkmalpflege aus praktischer und wissenschaftlicher Perspektive erwartet die Gäste. Von FLEX referieren: Cristoph Dijoux zum Projekt „ARsist: Augmented Reality basierte Assistenzsysteme für die Denkmalpflege“ (Donnerstag, 14:30 Uhr), Luisa Sander zum Projekt „ReFoRe: Recycling for Reuse. Bewertung und Aufbereitung von Altholz zur Rückführung in den Kreislauf“ (Freitag, 14:30 Uhr) und Benedikt Adrian zum Projekt „PreloadTimber: Einfluss druckinduzierter Vorbelastung und rheologischer Verformung auf die Zugfestigkeit von Bauholz“ (Samstag, 12 Uhr).
Weitere Vorträge und Workshops auf der „denkmal“
Im Kontext des Denkmalnetzes Sachsen wird Prof. Dr. Ulrich Weferling, HTWK-Professor für Vermessungskunde, am Donnerstag um 17 Uhr einen Vortrag zu seinem aktuellen studentischen Seminarprojekt an dem letzten erhaltenen Bauwerk des Spinnmühlenkomplexes in Wolkenburg, Limbach-Oberfrohna, halten (Halle 2, G38). Basierend auf einer detaillierten Bauaufnahme wurden die konstruktiven und gestalterischen Merkmale des Bauwerks aus dem beginnenden 19. Jahrhundert analysiert und damit wesentliche Aspekte der Baugeschichte geklärt.
Beim Workshop zur „Künstlichen Intelligenz und Denkmalpflege“ am Freitag um 10 Uhr (Mehrzweckfläche 3, Ebene 0) wird der KI-Einsatz im Denkmalmonitoring, in der restauratorischen Arbeitsweise und der Denkmalvermittlung vorgestellt. Bei der abschließenden Wrap-up-Diskussion ist Prof. Dr. Franziska Klemstein, Professorin für Data Lifecycle Management in Kultur- und Wissenschaftseinrichtungen, beteiligt. Eine Anmeldung zum Workshop ist bis 2. November 2026 möglich.
Hochschultag der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Nachhaltiges Bauen mit Messebesuch
Parallel zu beiden Messen veranstaltet die Deutsche Gesellschaft für Nachhaltiges Bauen (DGNB) in Kooperation mit der HTWK Leipzig ihren DGNB-Hochschultag erstmals in Leipzig. Rund 30 Fachleute der DGNB sowie Lehrende und Forschende von deutschen und einer Schweizer Hochschule tauschen sich zwei Tage zum Thema „Nachhaltiges Bauen in der Lehre“ aus. Am Donnerstag treffen sich die Beteiligten zum Austausch im Congress Center Leipzig (CCL) der Leipziger Messe im Rahmen der Denkmalmesse. Impulsvorträge halten dort unter anderem die HTWK-Professoren Björn Höhlig und Alexander Stahr. Der zweite Teil des DGNB findet am Freitag an der HTWK Leipzig statt.

Die TU Clausthal und die Babeș-Bolyai-Universität in Cluj-Napoca (Rumänien) vereinbaren ein Double-Degree-Programm.
Die Technische Universität Clausthal und die Babeș-Bolyai-Universität (UBB) in Cluj-Napoca, Rumänien, haben einen Kooperationsvertrag über ein Double-Degree-Programm im Bachelorstudiengang Informatik unterzeichnet. Studierende beider Hochschulen verbringen künftig einen Teil ihres Studiums an der Partneruniversität und erwerben am Ende zwei Abschlüsse: den Bachelor of Science der TU Clausthal und die rumänische Licență der UBB.
Das Programm richtet sich an der UBB an die Studierenden des deutschsprachigen Informatikzweigs der Fakultät für Mathematik und Informatik. Damit ist Deutsch an beiden Standorten die Unterrichtssprache. Das ist eine Besonderheit, die den Austausch für Studierende beider Seiten besonders attraktiv macht. Bewerbungen sind ab sofort möglich.
Entwickelt wurde das Programm von Prof. Christian Bartelt von der TU Clausthal (Institute for Software and Systems Engineering) und Prof. Christian Săcărea von der Fakultät für Mathematik und Informatik der UBB. Begleitet hat den Prozess Prof. Stefan Hartmann, Vizepräsident für Studium und Lehre der TU Clausthal.
„Mit dem Double-Degree-Programm schaffen wir für unsere Informatikstudierenden eine echte internationale Perspektive, ohne Sprachbarriere und mit zwei anerkannten Abschlüssen“, sagt Prof. Hartmann. „Die Babeș-Bolyai-Universität ist eine der renommiertesten Universitäten Rumäniens, und ihr deutschsprachiger Studienzweig passt hervorragend zu uns.“
„Deutschsprachige Bildung hat in Klausenburg und in ganz Siebenbürgen eine lange Tradition. Mit dem Double Degree führen wir sie in die Zukunft: Unser deutschsprachiger Informatik Studiengang wird zur Brücke zwischen Cluj-Napoca und Clausthal. Davon profitieren Studierende auf beiden Seiten, fachlich, sprachlich und persönlich. Mit der TU Clausthal haben wir dafür einen idealen Partner gefunden“, ergänzt Prof. Săcărea, auch Vizerektor der Babeș-Bolyai-Universität.
„Einerseits passt die inhaltliche Ausrichtung der über den Double-Degree verbundenen Informatikstudiengänge beider Universitäten hervorragend zueinander. Anderseits ergänzen sich beide Standorte in der persönlichen, naturnahen Studienatmosphäre der TU Clausthal mit dem lebendigen, kulturell vielfältigen Studienleben der europäischen Großstadt Klausenburg“, freut sich Prof. Bartelt. Der Clausthaler plant schon die Double-Degree-Initiative auf die neuen KI-Studiengänge zu „AI Engineering“ an beiden Universitäten auszuweiten.
Die Babeș-Bolyai-Universität in Cluj-Napoca (Klausenburg) ist mit rund 50.000 Studierenden die größte Universität Rumäniens und bietet Studiengänge in rumänischer, ungarischer, deutscher und englischer Sprache an.

title: Erster „Korea-Tag“ in Aachen: Kultur und Wirtschaft feiern vereint Erfolg
content:
Erster „Korea-Tag“ in Aachen: Kultur und Wirtschaft feiern vereint Erfolg
10. Oktober 2026, Aachen– Zum ersten Mal hat in Aachen der Korea-Tag stattgefunden – und mit über 300 Gästen aus der Region für einen gelungenen Auftakt gesorgt. Die koreanische Botschaft, Außenstelle Bonn, und die RWTH Aachen präsentierten am 10. Oktober 2026 ein facettenreiches Programm, das koreanische Kultur und deutsch-koreanische Wirtschaftskooperationen in den Fokus rückte. Die hohe Teilnehmerzahl und das durchweg positive Echo unterstreichen das große Interesse an dieser neuen Veranstaltungsreihe.
Brückenbauer zwischen Kultur und Wissenschaft: Gemeinsame Ziele des Korea-Tags
Der Korea-Tag wurde ins Leben gerufen, um die koreanische Kultur und die wirtschaftlichen Beziehungen zwischen Deutschland und Südkorea im Raum Aachen sichtbarer zu machen. Gleichzeitig sollte die Veranstaltung konkrete Brücken zwischen Hochschule, Unternehmen und koreanischen Institutionen schlagen. Die StädteRegion Aachen und Südkorea verbinden bereits enge Partnerschaften in den Bereichen Wirtschaft, Wissenschaft und Technologie – etwa durch die offizielle Zusammenarbeit der StädteRegion mit der südkoreanischen Stadt Ansan.
„Der Korea-Tag bietet eine wertvolle Gelegenheit, die wachsende Zusammenarbeit zwischen Korea und Deutschland hier in Aachen hautnah zu erleben“, betont Byun Chul-Hwan, Leiter des Bonner Büros der Botschaft der Republik Korea. Prof. Dr. Thomas Gries, Rektoratsbeauftragter der RWTH Aachen für die Zusammenarbeit mit Korea, ergänzt: „Als eine der forschungsstärksten Universitäten Europas sehen wir großes Potenzial in der vertieften Kooperation mit koreanischen Partnern – sowohl in der Lehre als auch in innovativen Forschungsprojekten.“
________________________________________
Ein Programm für alle Sinne: Von Innovation bis K-Pop
Das abwechslungsreiche Programm des ersten Korea-Tags umfasste fachliche Vorträge, kulturelle Highlights und Networking-Möglichkeiten:
• Begrüßung und Grußworte Begrüßt wurden die Gäste von Byun Chul-Hwan (koreanische Botschaft, Außenstelle Bonn) und Prof. Dr. Thomas Gries (RWTH Aachen).
• Fachvorträge unter dem Motto „Next Stop Korea“ Alumni der RWTH berichteten über ihre Erfahrungen in Korea, das International Office der Universität stellte seine Programme vor, und die Firma AGIT präsentierte erfolgreiche Unternehmenskooperationen.
• Podiumsdiskussion: „Deutschland und Korea – Partnerschaften für Innovation“ Expert:innen diskutierten über aktuelle Projekte und zukünftige Chancen der deutsch-koreanischen Zusammenarbeit.
• Kulturelle Beiträge Die Mezzosopranistin Ji Young Mennekes begeisterte mit traditionellen Gratulationsliedern, das „Town-K Dance Studio“ sorgte mit einer K-Pop-Tanzperformance für Gänsehaut. Weitere Highlights waren eine Hanbok-Fotostation, koreanische Kalligrafie, eine Gaming-Ecke sowie die kulinarische Reise durch die koreanische Küche.
• Networking und Austausch Aussteller wie das Korea Germany Technology Cooperation Center (KGTCC) und das Institut für Textiltechnik (ITA) der RWTH Aachen boten Gelegenheit zum persönlichen Austausch und zur Vertiefung von Kontakten.
________________________________________
Erfolgreicher Auftakt: RWTH plant Fortsetzung
Die durchweg positive Resonanz der ersten Auflage des Korea-Tags zeigt, dass das Format auf großes Interesse stößt. Die RWTH Aachen plant daher, die Veranstaltung in ähnlicher Form zu wiederholen – um die kulturellen und wirtschaftlichen Bande zwischen Aachen und Südkorea weiter zu stärken.
Hintergrund: Aachen und Südkorea – eine starke Partnerschaft
Die StädteRegion Aachen und die südkoreanische Stadt Ansan pflegen seit Jahren enge Beziehungen in den Bereichen Wirtschaft, Wissenschaft und Technologie. Die RWTH Aachen engagiert sich dabei besonders in der Forschungskooperation und dem studentischen Austausch. Der Korea-Tag knüpft an diese bestehenden Initiativen an und schafft eine Plattform für den multilateralen Dialog.
